1.q: How is the level of backflow protection chosen for a particular connection?
o: It is set by the length of the pipe run to the outlet under normal working conditions
It is decided by the colour of the pipe being used on site
It is matched to the fluid category, so higher risks get greater protection
It is fixed at the same low level for every situation on site
1.w: Protection is selected according to the fluid risk category; the more hazardous the fluid, the stronger the protection required.

n.0: Pipe length does not determine the required protection level.
n.1: Pipe colour aids identification but does not set protection.
n.3: One fixed low level would not cover higher-risk situations.

1.q: Why is backflow treated as a serious hazard to the public supply?
o: It can pull contaminants into treated water that people then drink
It slows the delivery of water to properties at the end of the main
It makes the water look cloudy but leaves it perfectly safe to drink
It only wastes a small amount of water at the point of the fitting
1.w: Reverse flow can carry dirty or chemical-laden water into the drinking supply, so it is a public health risk.

n.1: Backflow is a contamination risk, not merely a delivery-speed problem.
n.2: The danger is unsafe water, not just appearance; it can be genuinely harmful.
n.3: The harm is contamination of many users, not a little wasted water.

1.q: Measuring residual chlorine both when dosing and after the hold lets the operative see:
o: How far the water level has dropped inside the main as the work is being signed off
How much of the chlorine has been used up during the contact time
How many customers were using their taps during the hold
How much the pipe has expanded since it was first filled
1.w: Comparing the two readings shows the demand and whether enough chlorine remained.

n.0: Residual readings measure chlorine, not the water level in the main.
n.2: The residual comparison is a chlorine check, not a count of customers.
n.3: Residual readings track chlorine, not any expansion of the pipe.

1.q: Human sewage getting into the water supply is dangerous mainly because it carries:
o: Only harmless dissolved minerals and trace salts
Nothing worse than a slightly cloudy colour
Disease-causing bacteria, viruses and protozoa
Approved disinfectant chemicals for the main
1.w: Sewage carries harmful micro-organisms that can cause serious waterborne disease.

n.0: Sewage carries harmful organisms, not just minerals.
n.1: The danger is the organisms, not appearance.
n.3: Sewage is a contaminant, not a disinfectant.

1.q: Why should a trench be kept as clean and dry as possible before laying the main?
o: So the excavator can reach a greater depth before the shift ends
So the trench looks tidy for any passing members of the public
So dirt and foul water cannot get into the pipe as it is laid
So less imported bedding material is needed at the end of the job
1.w: A clean, dry trench stops dirt and foul water getting into the pipe while it is being laid.

n.0: Cleanliness is about contamination, not digging depth.
n.1: Appearance is not the reason for keeping the trench clean.
n.3: Saving bedding is not why the trench is kept clean and dry.

1.q: Bacteria and viruses that cause waterborne disease mainly come from which source?
o: Clean topsoil taken from a domestic garden
Approved, certified potable pipe lubricant and paste
Sewage and foul water in and around the works
New, unopened, bagged plastic pipe fittings
1.w: The main source of harmful bacteria and viruses is sewage and foul water.

n.0: Soil is a source but foul water carries the worst.
n.1: Approved products are not a source of organisms.
n.3: Clean stored fittings carry no sewage organisms.

1.q: Which best explains why leaching is a problem in drinking water pipes?
o: The pipe becomes weaker and splits open
Chemicals pass from the material into the water
The water pressure inside gradually builds up higher
The pipe changes colour on the outside
1.w: Leaching means chemicals move from the material into the water people drink.

n.0: Splitting is not what leaching means.
n.2: A pressure build-up is not what leaching means.
n.3: External colour change is not what leaching means.

1.q: Why should flushing be done at a good flow rate rather than a slow trickle?
o: A trickle uses more chlorine than a fast flow does
A good flow rate scours out loose dirt more effectively
A slow trickle of water raises the pressure right across the network
Fast flushing is only ever needed on brand-new mains
1.w: A good flow rate creates enough velocity to scour and carry away loose dirt and debris from the repaired main.

n.0: Flow rate is about scouring, not chlorine use.
n.2: Flushing does not raise network pressure.
n.3: Effective flushing applies to repairs, not just new mains.

1.q: A burst main is repaired but debris is left inside the pipe. The main public-health concern is that:
o: The repair will probably need repainting again within the year
Consumers could be supplied with contaminated water
The water pressure gauge may read slightly high
The road surface above may crack over time
1.w: Debris left in a main risks supplying contaminated water.

n.0: Repainting is not a public-health concern.
n.2: A gauge reading is not the main health concern.
n.3: Road cracking is not the drinking-water concern.

1.q: If a trench floods with water during a repair, what should be done?
o: Carry on jointing while the open pipe ends still sit beneath the water
Leave the water in place as it keeps the pipe cool
De-water the trench so the pipe ends stay out of the water
Add more water to dilute any dirt that has collected
1.w: A flooded trench must be de-watered (pumped or bailed out) so the open pipe ends are not sitting in contaminated water.

n.0: Jointing under water lets contamination into the main.
n.1: Leaving flood water risks it entering the open pipe.
n.3: Adding water increases the flooding and the contamination risk.

1.q: A water company must be able to show the Drinking Water Inspectorate that its water is:
o: Cheaper than a rival supplier's water
Being sold in the very largest volumes
Meeting the required safety standards
Coloured to reveal where it came from
1.w: Companies must demonstrate to the DWI that their water meets the required safety standards.

n.0: Price comparisons are not what the DWI requires.
n.1: Volume sold is not the DWI's standard.
n.3: Drinking water is not coloured, and colour is not a DWI standard.

1.q: Good water control at a repair supports hygiene by ensuring that:
o: The main stays live and pressurised throughout the cut
Trench water is deliberately fed through the new joint
No pump or bailing is ever needed on any job
The excavation stays dry and the pipe ends stay clean
1.w: Controlling the water keeps the excavation dry and the open pipe ends clean, which protects the supply.

n.0: The section is isolated and depressurised while worked on.
n.1: Trench water must never be fed through the joint.
n.2: Pumping or bailing is often required to keep the trench dry.

1.q: Which is the safest choice of thread sealant on a drinking water fitting?
o: A sealant approved for potable water
A sealant normally used on central heating
A sealant made for guttering joints
A sealant intended for roofing work
1.w: Only a sealant approved for potable water should be used on drinking water.

n.1: A heating sealant is not approved for drinking water.
n.2: A guttering sealant is not approved for drinking water.
n.3: A roofing sealant is not approved for drinking water.

1.q: Which of these is the most serious possible consequence of backflow into a public main?
o: A slightly higher electricity cost at the pumping station
A short delay in filling a tank on one site
An outbreak of illness among people who drink the water
A small stain left on the inside of one pipe
1.w: The gravest consequence is a public health outbreak from contaminated drinking water.

n.0: Pumping costs are trivial next to a health outbreak.
n.1: A filling delay is minor compared with illness.
n.3: A pipe stain is insignificant against a health risk.

1.q: If a pipe cap or plug is lost on site, the best action is to:
o: Leave the pipe open and simply lay it more quickly than planned
Stuff the end with a rag from the van to keep the worst out
Fit a proper replacement cap before leaving the pipe end open
Tip the pipe downward so that nothing can settle inside the end
1.w: A proper replacement cap is fitted so the end is never left open to contamination.

n.0: Laying quickly still leaves the end open to dirt.
n.1: A rag is not a clean, reliable seal for the pipe.
n.3: Tipping the pipe still leaves the end open to foul water.

1.q: Why must pipes, fittings and tools be kept clean during clean-water work?
o: To make the pipe fittings easier to push together properly
To keep the tools from rusting in the trench
To stop dirt and germs getting into the drinking water
To help the pipe joints look neat when finished
1.w: Anything on the pipe, fitting or tool can be washed into the main and contaminate the drinking water.

n.0: Ease of assembly is not the reason cleanliness is required.
n.1: Preventing rust is a maintenance point, not the hygiene reason.
n.3: A tidy appearance is not why cleanliness matters here.

1.q: Keeping the trench free of standing water protects mainly against:
o: germs and dirt entering the new main
the pipe sinking below the design level
the excavator getting bogged down
delays waiting for the ground to firm up
1.w: The purpose of de-watering is hygiene: keeping germs and dirt out of the drinking-water main.

n.1: Pipe level is a separate setting-out issue.
n.2: Machine access is not the hygiene reason.
n.3: Programme delays are not the hygiene purpose.

1.q: A worker wants a quick sandwich but has handled pipework in a wet chamber. What should they do first?
o: Simply wipe their hands down the front of their overalls
Eat it as quickly as they can so the food is exposed less
Only bother washing if the sandwich is completely unwrapped
Wash their hands thoroughly before touching the food
1.w: They must wash their hands thoroughly before handling any food.

n.0: Wiping on dirty overalls does not remove the organisms.
n.1: Eating fast does not protect against contaminated hands.
n.2: Handling food with dirty hands is a risk whether wrapped or not.

1.q: Scenario: you have a tanker of strong chlorinated water from disinfecting a main. Before discharge you should:
o: Neutralise the chlorine so it is safe to release without harming the environment
Tip it straight into the nearest surface drain to save time according to the operative on site
Pour it back into the disinfected main ready for the customer
Add extra chlorine to make sure it is fully sterilised first
1.w: The chlorine is chemically neutralised first so the discharge does no environmental harm.

n.1: Strong chlorinated water is neutralised first; it is never simply tipped away.
n.2: Chlorinated waste is not returned to a main destined for supply.
n.3: Adding more chlorine makes disposal worse, not safer.

1.q: What is the common name for the card issued under the National Water Hygiene scheme?
o: The Green Card, used for general construction skills
The Gold Card, held by qualified site managers
The Blue Card, which shows water hygiene competence
The Red Card, issued to trainees while on site
1.w: The scheme issues the Blue Card, confirming the holder has passed the water hygiene assessment.

n.0: The Green Card relates to construction skills, not the National Water Hygiene scheme.
n.1: A Gold Card is not the card issued by the National Water Hygiene scheme.
n.3: The scheme does not issue a red trainee card for water hygiene.

1.q: Contamination is most likely to enter the network at points where:
o: The main runs sealed underground
The water is under full pressure
Valves are shut and fully intact
The pipe is opened up or is cut into
1.w: Opening or cutting into a main exposes the inside and is where contamination gets in.

n.0: Sealed intact pipe keeps contamination out.
n.1: Full pressure helps keep contamination out.
n.2: Intact valves are not an entry point.

1.q: How does washing your hands protect the public who drink the water?
o: It makes the water coming out of the tap taste much sweeter during ordinary operations on the network
It noticeably increases the pressure inside the water main
It speeds up the flow of the water through the pipe
It stops organisms on your hands reaching the potable supply
1.w: Clean hands stop organisms reaching the potable supply the public drinks.

n.0: Hand washing has no effect on the taste of the water.
n.1: Hand hygiene does not change water pressure.
n.2: Hand washing does not affect flow rate in the pipe.

1.q: Which action risks letting sewage-contaminated water into the new main?
o: Capping the pipe ends firmly whenever the crew stop for a break
Laying an uncapped pipe end down into foul water in the trench
Pumping the trench out and directing the discharge well away
Storing spare fittings on clean boarding clear of the wet ground
1.w: Laying an uncapped end into foul water lets the sewage-contaminated water straight into the main.

n.0: Capping the ends keeps foul water out, not in.
n.2: Pumping the discharge away keeps the trench clear.
n.3: Clean, dry storage keeps fittings uncontaminated.

1.q: A burst main has soaked the surrounding ground with sewage from a nearby damaged sewer. This means:
o: Extra care and thorough disinfection are especially vital
The repair can proceed exactly as any normal job
No flushing is needed here because sewage is mostly just water
The main can return to supply without a sample
1.w: Sewage contamination makes thorough water control, disinfection, flushing and sampling especially important.

n.1: Sewage contamination raises the risk and demands extra care.
n.2: Sewage makes flushing and disinfection more important, not less.
n.3: A sample is more clearly needed, not less, in these conditions.

1.q: Personal hygiene is said to protect 'both the water and the worker'. The worker part refers to:
o: Not catching diseases such as Weil's disease from the work
Earning a small bonus for keeping a tidy and clean worksite
Avoiding too much general wear and tear on their work boots
Being the first person in the queue at the site canteen
1.w: The worker part means not catching diseases such as Weil's disease from the work.

n.1: Protecting the worker means their health, not a tidiness bonus.
n.2: It refers to the worker's health, not their footwear.
n.3: It is about avoiding illness, not canteen queues.

2.q: How should a standpipe and hose be stored between jobs to stay hygienic?
o: Thrown loose in the van footwell with other tools
Left outside on the ground overnight to air off
Coiled around a dirty wheel to keep them tidy on the day
Kept clean with the open ends protected from dirt
2.w: Clean storage with protected ends keeps contamination away from the fittings.

n.0: Loose storage lets the ends pick up dirt and grease.
n.1: Leaving them on the ground exposes the ends to contamination.
n.2: A dirty wheel would transfer contamination to the fittings.

2.q: Why is a healthy-seeming worker with a recent stomach bug still a risk to potable water?
o: They will by now have completely forgotten their hygiene training
They can still carry and spread organisms while recovering
All of their hand tools will have rusted while they were off sick
They are certain to work far too quickly and make mistakes
2.w: A recovering worker may still carry and shed organisms into the water.

n.0: Recovery does not erase training; the risk is carrying organisms.
n.2: Rusty tools are not the concern; carriage of pathogens is.
n.3: Work speed is not the issue; possible carriage of organisms is.

2.q: If a product's approval cannot be confirmed on site, you should:
o: use it and confirm approval afterwards
use it because the time is short
use it if similar ones were approved
not use it until approval is confirmed
2.w: Do not use a product until its approval for drinking water is confirmed.

n.0: Confirming later can leave contaminated water in use.
n.1: Being short of time does not allow its use.
n.2: Similar products being approved does not confirm it.

2.q: Pumping water out of a trench should be done:
o: so it discharges away from the open pipe
straight back down into the open pipe end again
into the next section still to be laid
over the fittings stored beside the dig
2.w: The discharge is directed away so the removed water cannot run back into the pipe or over clean fittings.

n.1: Discharging into the pipe defeats the purpose entirely.
n.2: Sending it into the next section spreads the water.
n.3: Wetting stored fittings contaminates them too.

2.q: Which of the following is NOT a purpose of the Water Supply (Water Fittings) Regulations 1999?
o: Preventing the contamination of the water
Preventing the wasteful loss of the water
Preventing the misuse of the water supply
Setting the country's national minimum wage
2.w: The regulations prevent contamination, waste and misuse; they do not set the minimum wage.

n.0: This is a genuine purpose of the regulations.
n.1: Preventing waste is a genuine purpose of the regulations.
n.2: Preventing misuse is a genuine purpose of the regulations.

2.q: After recovering from diarrhoea and vomiting, what may an employer require before you resume work?
o: A full retake of your manual handling lifting test
That you buy your own replacement set of work gloves
Attendance at a toolbox talk all about ladder safety
Health screening to confirm you are fit to return
2.w: Employers may require health screening to confirm fitness before you resume potable work.

n.0: Manual handling is not the clearance needed after a gut illness.
n.1: Buying gloves is not the health-clearance step required.
n.2: A ladder talk is unrelated to clearing you after illness.

2.q: Rust flakes and pipe scale come loose inside an old main. These are:
o: Chemical contamination to be neutralised
Physical contamination that should be flushed
Microbiological contamination to be dosed
Safe to leave since they will soon settle
2.w: Loose rust and scale are solid debris, a physical contaminant to be flushed out.

n.0: Rust flakes are solid debris, not a dosed chemical.
n.2: They are not living organisms.
n.3: Loose debris must be removed, not left.

2.q: A customer reports a strange taste days after a repair. You should first suspect:
o: the mains pressure being too high
a material used that was not approved
the pipe being buried a little too deep
the stop tap being left half open
2.w: A taste change after a repair points to an unapproved material contaminating water.

n.0: High pressure does not taint the water's taste.
n.2: Burial depth does not taint the water's taste.
n.3: A half-open stop tap does not taint the water.

2.q: The National Water Hygiene assessment is aimed at people who work on:
o: building hot and cold water services only
swimming pool and spa circulation systems
industrial cooling towers and chiller systems
the public clean (potable) water supply
2.w: The scheme covers work on the public clean (potable) water supply.

n.0: The scheme is about the public supply, not building hot and cold systems.
n.1: Pool and spa systems are outside the National Water Hygiene scheme.
n.2: Cooling towers are not covered by the National Water Hygiene scheme.

2.q: Before starting a job that could contaminate the mains, an operative must:
o: hold a valid National Water Hygiene card
obtain written permission from the local police
pass a separate confined space medical first
register the job with the local fire service
2.w: A valid card is required before such restricted work.

n.1: Police permission is not required for this work.
n.2: A confined space medical is a separate matter.
n.3: The fire service does not authorise this work.

2.q: A worker who deliberately contaminates a drinking main risks:
o: Being criminally prosecuted as an individual
Receiving a guaranteed rise in their pay
Getting an automatic promotion at work
Being allowed a much longer lunch break
2.w: Deliberate contamination can result in the individual facing criminal prosecution.

n.1: There is no reward; the risk is prosecution.
n.2: Contamination leads to penalties, not promotion.
n.3: This trivialises what is a serious criminal matter.

2.q: If insects or leaves get into an open pipe end, the operative should:
o: leave them as they will decay away
joint the pipe and forget about them
flush them along to the next length
clean them out before the pipe is used
2.w: Anything that gets into the bore is removed before use so it cannot contaminate the water.

n.0: Leaving them to decay contaminates the main.
n.1: Jointing over them traps contamination inside.
n.2: Flushing them along still leaves them in the system.

2.q: Which best completes the sequence: disinfect, check residual, ___, sample?
o: Swab the main to remove the leftover debris once the pipe has been rejoined
Charge the main with a second dose of chlorine
Flush the strong chlorinated water out of the main
Bring the main straight into customer supply
2.w: After the residual check, the main is flushed before the passing sample is taken.

n.0: Swabbing happens first, not between the residual check and sampling.
n.1: A second dose is not part of the standard sequence here.
n.3: Supply comes after the passing sample, not before flushing.

2.q: A worker gets a headache, fever and muscle pain a week after a wet chamber. What should they consider?
o: That it is simply ordinary tiredness and can be ignored
That they merely need to drink a lot more water than usual
That it could be early Weil's disease and needs a doctor
That it is certain to be an allergic reaction to their gloves
2.w: Flu-like symptoms after wet work could be early Weil's disease and need a doctor.

n.0: Flu-like symptoms after wet work should not be brushed off as tiredness.
n.1: Rehydration alone is not the answer to possible Weil's disease.
n.3: A glove allergy would not explain fever and muscle pain after wet work.

2.q: Cryptosporidiosis in drinking water is caused by:
o: A bacterium that is easily killed by chlorine
A protozoan parasite called Cryptosporidium
A common airborne virus spread by coughing
A mould that grows inside old lead pipes
2.w: Cryptosporidiosis is caused by the protozoan Cryptosporidium.

n.0: Cryptosporidium is a resistant parasite, not that bacterium.
n.2: Cryptosporidiosis is not an airborne coughing virus.
n.3: It is not caused by mould in pipes.

2.q: An authorised standpipe user finds the nearest hydrant is not on their permit area. They should:
o: Only use a hydrant they are actually authorised to use
Use it anyway since all hydrants carry the same water
Use it and note the location for the paperwork later
Use it briefly as long as no one from the area sees on the day
2.w: Authorisation is specific, so the user must keep to hydrants they are permitted to use.

n.1: Authorisation is specific and does not cover every hydrant.
n.2: Recording it afterwards does not make the use authorised.
n.3: Whether or not they are seen has no bearing on authority.

2.q: A burst on a busy road has debris and traffic dirt around it. Why treat this as a contamination risk?
o: Traffic dirt sterilises the pipe and needs no attention
Road debris cannot physically reach an open pipe end
Only rural bursts, never urban ones, risk contamination
Road debris and dirt can be washed into the open main
2.w: Debris and dirt from a road surface can be washed or knocked into the exposed main just like any other soil.

n.0: Traffic dirt contaminates rather than sterilises the pipe.
n.1: Debris can readily reach an open end in the trench.
n.2: Urban and rural bursts both carry a contamination risk.

2.q: What should an operative do first if they see raw sewage near an open drinking main?
o: Finish making the connection as quickly as they can
Stop work and report the risk immediately
Take a short break and come back to it later
Carry on with the work and say nothing at all
2.w: The immediate step is to stop and report the serious contamination risk.

n.0: Rushing the connection could draw contamination into the main.
n.2: Delaying leaves a serious risk unaddressed.
n.3: Ignoring the risk endangers public health.

2.q: Which of the following would count as a cross-connection to avoid?
o: A drinking-water pipe joined to another drinking-water pipe
A drinking-water pipe fitted with an approved double check valve on site
A drinking-water pipe protected by a proper air gap
A drinking-water pipe joined to a pipe carrying recycled grey water
2.w: Linking potable pipe to grey water allows contamination to cross over, which is exactly what must be avoided.

n.0: Joining two potable pipes is not a cross-connection hazard.
n.1: A double check valve is protection, not an unguarded cross-connection.
n.2: An air gap is protection against, not an example of, a cross-connection.

2.q: A contractor asks whether disinfection can be skipped on a planned main renewal. The correct position is:
o: It cannot be skipped, because the new main has been open and must be disinfected first
It can be skipped because planned work is always cleaner than repairs
It can be skipped as long as the pipe was delivered in a wrapper
It can be skipped provided the contractor signs a short form as the work is being signed off
2.w: A renewed main has been open to the surroundings, so it is disinfected before supply.

n.1: Planned or not, an opened main is disinfected before it is supplied.
n.2: Delivery wrapping does not remove the need to disinfect after installation.
n.3: No form removes the requirement to disinfect an opened main.

2.q: A drinking water main and a contaminated source are close together. The law expects the operative to:
o: Connect the two of them together to save buying new pipe
Leave both of them open to the surrounding air
Mix the two so that the pressure is balanced
Keep the drinking water protected from contamination
2.w: The operative must keep drinking water protected, as required by law and good practice.

n.0: Connecting a clean main to a contaminated source risks a criminal offence.
n.1: Leaving mains open invites contamination.
n.2: Mixing clean and contaminated water is never acceptable.

2.q: The main danger where a sewer passes close to a clean-water pipe is:
o: Foul contents leaking across into the drinking-water main
The sewer making the water main harder to trace with equipment
The two pipes settling at slightly different rates over the years
The sewer taking up the room needed for the water main's bedding
2.w: The main danger is foul contents leaking from the sewer into the drinking-water main.

n.1: Tracing difficulty is not the real danger here.
n.2: Different settlement is a minor engineering point.
n.3: Bedding room is not the chief hazard from a close sewer.

2.q: If a member of the public reports brown water from their tap, the ultimate regulator of that quality issue is:
o: The operative's own line manager
The Drinking Water Inspectorate
The manufacturer of the pipe
The local passenger bus company
2.w: The Drinking Water Inspectorate is the regulator overseeing drinking water quality.

n.0: A line manager is not the national water quality regulator.
n.2: Manufacturers make products but do not regulate quality.
n.3: A bus company has no water regulatory role.

2.q: An operative wants to rest the open pipe end on the spoil heap for a moment. This is:
o: Wrong, because spoil will contaminate the inside of the pipe
Fine, because spoil is always clean, dry material
Advised, because the spoil supports the pipe safely
Acceptable, provided it is only for a short time
2.w: Resting an open end on the spoil heap lets soil and germs into the pipe, so it should never be done.

n.1: Spoil is dirty ground material, not clean.
n.2: Supporting the pipe must not involve contaminating its interior.
n.3: Even brief contact with spoil can contaminate the pipe.

2.q: You realise a new fitting was dropped in the mud but a colleague has already jointed it in. You should:
o: Say nothing, since the fitting is now sealed in place
Raise it so the section can be cleaned, disinfected and flushed
Wait to see whether the final sample happens to pass
Note it for the records but take no action on site
2.w: A muddy fitting jointed into the main is a contamination risk, so it must be flagged and the section cleaned, disinfected and flushed.

n.0: Sealing in a dirty fitting leaves contamination in the supply.
n.2: Hoping the sample passes ignores a known contamination event.
n.3: Recording it is not enough; the contamination must be dealt with.

3.q: The Drinking Water Inspectorate helps to ensure that tap water is:
o: Safe and wholesome for people to drink
Provided free of charge to households
Sold at exactly the same price everywhere
Supplied to homes in sealed bottles
3.w: The DWI's purpose is to ensure drinking water is safe and wholesome for the public.

n.1: The DWI does not make water free; it checks its safety.
n.2: Pricing is not the DWI's role.
n.3: The DWI oversees mains water quality, not bottled delivery.

3.q: If left untreated, Weil's disease can progress to which serious conditions?
o: Broken bones together with dislocated joints
A permanent loss of the person's sense of smell
A slow but total loss of the person's eyesight
Jaundice and kidney or liver failure
3.w: Untreated, it can progress to jaundice and kidney or liver failure.

n.0: It does not cause broken bones; it can cause organ failure.
n.1: Loss of smell is not a recognised progression of the disease.
n.2: Blindness is not the described serious outcome; organ failure is.

3.q: Why must operatives take contamination risks so seriously on the clean-water network?
o: Even a small mistake can affect the health of many people
Because mistakes only ever affect one single house
Because the water company will always spot it first
Because any contamination will clear itself within a few short hours
3.w: A small error can put many people's health at risk.

n.1: Mistakes can affect far more than one house.
n.2: You cannot rely on the mistake being spotted first.
n.3: Contamination does not reliably clear on its own.

3.q: Foul water has seeped into the trench from a nearby drain. The safe action is to:
o: stop, remove the water and deal with the source
carry on laying as the pipe is sealed anyway
bail a little out and lay between seepages
lay the pipe a little higher to keep it just clear
3.w: Foul seepage is a serious risk, so work stops, the water is removed and the source is dealt with before laying.

n.1: An open end means the pipe is not sealed against foul water.
n.2: Bailing between seepages still leaves foul water present.
n.3: Raising the pipe does not remove the foul-water hazard.

3.q: When recommissioning a repaired main, why is it filled slowly and carefully?
o: To avoid disturbing sediment and trapping air in the main
To make the job take as long as reasonably possible
To force trapped air deeper into the customer's pipes
To raise the pressure in the main well above the normal working level
3.w: Slow, careful filling avoids stirring up sediment and helps air escape rather than being trapped in the main.

n.1: Careful filling is about quality, not simply taking longer.
n.2: Slow filling helps air escape, not push it into customer pipes.
n.3: Recommissioning restores normal pressure, not an excessive one.

3.q: Which best describes good hygiene housekeeping on a clean-water site?
o: Old overalls, muddy hands and some loose spoil
Any overalls as long as work gets done
Dirty kit kept close by to save on walking
Clean overalls, clean hands and a tidy area
3.w: Clean overalls, clean hands and a tidy area together keep contamination away from the main.

n.0: Muddy hands and loose spoil spread contamination.
n.1: Ignoring hygiene to finish work risks the supply.
n.2: Keeping dirty kit close brings dirt to the pipe.

3.q: Scenario: a trainee asks what 'super-chlorinated' water is. The best answer is water that has been:
o: Left in the sun until the chlorine naturally became stronger
Dosed with chlorine well above normal supply strength to disinfect the main
Passed through the swab several times to pick up chlorine for the customer supplied by that main
Cooled below freezing so the chlorine concentrates at the top
3.w: Super-chlorinated means a high chlorine strength used for disinfection, far above drinking levels.

n.0: Super-chlorination is a deliberate high dose, not a result of sunlight.
n.2: The swab does not chlorinate the water; a high dose does.
n.3: Super-chlorination is about a high dose, not freezing or concentrating.

3.q: Which statement about card renewal is correct?
o: the assessment is re-taken every three years
the card stays valid for the holder's lifetime
renewal happens automatically each single year
renewal only needs a line manager's signature
3.w: The assessment must be re-taken every three years.

n.1: The card is not valid for life.
n.2: Renewal is not automatic each year.
n.3: Renewal needs the assessment, not a signature.

3.q: Reporting a hydrant fault promptly mainly protects:
o: The operative's own set of personal tools on the day
The appearance of the street where it sits
The fuel used by the works vehicle that day
The public who rely on that water being safe
3.w: Prompt reporting protects the public who depend on a safe supply.

n.0: Reporting is about the supply, not the operative's tools.
n.1: Street appearance is not why faults are reported.
n.2: Fuel use is unrelated to reporting a hydrant fault.

3.q: Backflow can occur even when the mains supply is working normally. Which situation still allows it?
o: The pressure on the customer's side becomes higher than the mains pressure
The mains pressure stays well above the pressure at every appliance
The water in the main is flowing steadily towards the customer
The customer's stop tap has been fully closed for the day
3.w: If pressure on the customer side climbs above the main (back-pressure), water can be pushed back in even with a healthy main.

n.1: When the main stays higher, flow is held in the correct direction.
n.2: Steady flow towards the customer is normal delivery, not backflow.
n.3: A closed stop tap isolates the property and prevents flow either way.

3.q: A hose or washer of the wrong type on a main could:
o: make the main run at a much higher pressure
add taste, odour or bacteria to the water
reduce the diameter of the pipe bore
change the colour of the pipe outside
3.w: Wrong washers and hoses can taint water or support bacteria, contaminating it.

n.0: Higher pressure is not the contamination risk here.
n.2: A smaller bore is not the contamination risk here.
n.3: External colour is not the contamination risk here.

3.q: If a hydrant is found to be damaged or leaking, the operative should:
o: Ignore it, as someone else will notice it later
Attempt a permanent repair using their own tools
Report it to the right person as soon as possible
Cover it over and carry on with the day's work on the day
3.w: Faults must be reported promptly so they can be dealt with properly.

n.0: Assuming others will report it can leave a fault unfixed.
n.1: Operatives should report faults, not carry out repairs.
n.3: Hiding a fault leaves the supply and public at risk.

3.q: Scenario: You notice the double check valve on a returned standpipe is faulty. You should:
o: Report the fault so the standpipe is not reused unsafely
Put it back on the shelf and say nothing if time is short
Leave a loose note only you would understand that morning
Use it once more yourself before mentioning it on the day
3.w: Reporting the fault stops the unsafe standpipe being used again.

n.1: Silently returning it lets it be reused without protection.
n.2: An unclear note may never reach the right person.
n.3: Using a faulty valve first still risks the supply.

3.q: Why is personal hygiene and care so important for someone working on the clean-water network?
o: It only matters for the appearance of the finished job
A single lapse can put many consumers' health at risk
It has no real effect on the water in the pipe
It just makes the paperwork easier to complete
3.w: One lapse in hygiene can endanger many consumers.

n.0: Hygiene is about health, not just appearance.
n.2: Hygiene directly affects water safety.
n.3: Hygiene is about protecting the public, not paperwork.

3.q: Why must every operative take backflow seriously even on a small job?
o: A single lapse can contaminate the supply for many people
A small job never involves any water at all
A small job is checked twice by a supervisor on a typical job
A small job uses only bottled water on site
3.w: Even a minor task can create a backflow path that pollutes the shared supply, so the risk is always real.

n.1: Small water jobs still involve water and carry the risk.
n.2: Double-checking is not guaranteed and does not remove the hazard.
n.3: Small jobs still use mains water, not only bottled water.

3.q: Flushing a main after disinfection removes the heavily chlorinated water so that:
o: The chlorine can be sold back to the supplier for a refund
Customers are not supplied with water that is too strong in chlorine to drink
The main can be left empty and out of use permanently according to the operative on site
The swab has more room to move around inside the pipe
3.w: Super-chlorinated water is unsuitable for supply, so it is flushed out first.

n.0: Flushing disposes of chlorinated water; it is not resold for money.
n.2: Flushing prepares the main for supply, not for permanent disuse.
n.3: The swab is recovered earlier; flushing clears chlorinated water.

3.q: New pipes and fittings waiting to be laid should be stored so that they are:
o: Lying in the bottom of the trench ready to be jointed quickly
Close to the spoil heap so that they are easy to reach when needed
Kept off foul ground and away from any contamination on the site
Left uncapped so the crew can check inside them at any moment
3.w: Pipes and fittings are kept off foul ground and clear of contamination until they are laid.

n.0: The trench floor is often wet and dirty, not a safe store.
n.1: The spoil heap is dirty ground, not a clean storage place.
n.3: Uncapped ends let dirt and foul water into the fittings.

3.q: Which of these is the best reason to use indicator organisms rather than testing for every possible pathogen?
o: Indicators make the water taste noticeably better
Indicators reliably signal a contamination risk more simply
Indicators remove the need to treat the water
Indicators guarantee the water is completely pure
3.w: Indicators give a simpler, reliable warning of contamination.

n.0: Indicators do not affect taste.
n.2: Indicators do not replace water treatment.
n.3: Indicators do not guarantee purity.

3.q: The best time to make sure the trench is clean and de-watered is:
o: After the pipe has been jointed and the trench is being backfilled
Before and during pipe-laying, so nothing dirty gets into the main
Only if an inspector is expected to visit the site during the day
At the very end of the job when the surface is being reinstated
3.w: The trench must be clean and dry before and during pipe-laying so nothing dirty enters the main.

n.0: After jointing is too late to protect the pipe interior.
n.2: Cleanliness is needed whether or not an inspector attends.
n.3: At reinstatement the pipe is already laid and cannot be protected.

3.q: Waterborne diseases are mainly passed on when:
o: Water is stored inside a metal container for a whole day
Water travels a long way through the mains
Water is left a little warmer than is usual
Human or animal waste gets into the drinking water
3.w: They spread when faecal waste contaminates drinking water.

n.0: Storing in metal does not spread these diseases.
n.1: Distance travelled does not itself spread disease.
n.2: A little extra warmth alone does not spread them.

3.q: Foul water and sewage are dangerous sources of contamination because they contain:
o: Only clean, dissolved and harmless minerals
Large numbers of disease-causing micro-organisms
Approved network disinfectant in solution
Nothing at all that could ever cause harm
3.w: Sewage carries high numbers of harmful micro-organisms, making it the most dangerous source.

n.0: It carries harmful organisms, not just minerals.
n.2: Sewage is a hazard, not a disinfectant.
n.3: It is one of the most harmful sources on site.

3.q: Short scenario: the trench has filled with muddy water after rain. You should:
o: lay the pipe and let the water drain past it
lay the pipe quickly while the water is shallow
add stone until the water is out of sight
pump it out before laying any pipe
3.w: Muddy water must be pumped out so pipe is laid on a clean, water-free bed.

n.0: Laying in the water lets contamination reach the pipe.
n.1: Shallow water is still a contamination risk.
n.2: Burying water under stone leaves foul water in the trench.

3.q: Which of these must you NOT do inside an excavation or trench?
o: Eat, drink or smoke
Wear your safety helmet
Keep your gloves on
Follow the dig plan
3.w: You must never eat, drink or smoke inside an excavation or trench.

n.1: Wearing your helmet is required, not forbidden.
n.2: Keeping gloves on is good practice, not something banned.
n.3: Following the plan is expected, not prohibited.

3.q: You have only trench water to hand and the fittings need rinsing. You should:
o: Use the dirty trench water rather than delay the repair
Rinse the fittings once and joint them quickly
Skip rinsing entirely and fit them as they are
Use clean water and disinfection, not trench water
3.w: Fittings must be cleaned with clean water and disinfected; trench water is contaminated and must never be used.

n.0: Trench water would contaminate the fittings, not clean them.
n.1: A single rinse in dirty water still leaves contamination.
n.2: Fitting dirty items builds contamination into the main.

3.q: The main reason flushing follows the residual check is to:
o: Refill the main with the same strong chlorine a second time
Cool the pipe down before the swab is sent through it before the main is put back into use
Raise the chlorine level higher than the procedure allows
Clear the disinfecting chlorine out once it has done its job in the main
3.w: After confirming the chlorine held, it is flushed away so the water is fit to sample and supply.

n.0: Flushing removes the chlorine; it does not refill with more.
n.1: The swab and cooling are not part of the post-disinfection flush.
n.2: Flushing lowers the chlorine, it does not push it higher.

4.q: The residual chlorine reading is taken using:
o: A test that shows the amount of chlorine left in a water sample
A tape measure run along the outside of the new main
A stopwatch timing how long the swab took to pass through
A thermometer pushed into the soil beside the pipe according to the operative on site
4.w: A simple chlorine test on the water gives the residual figure the operative records.

n.1: Residual chlorine is measured chemically on the water, not with a tape.
n.2: A stopwatch times events; it does not measure chlorine residual.
n.3: Soil temperature does not give the chlorine residual reading.

4.q: Why does the wrong grease sometimes lead to bacterial growth in a main?
o: It can act as a nutrient for bacteria
It makes the water colder inside
It raises the pressure in the pipe
It slows down the flow rate at the outlet
4.w: Some greases provide nutrients that allow bacteria to grow in the water.

n.1: Colder water is not why bacteria grow.
n.2: Higher pressure is not why bacteria grow.
n.3: Slower flow is not why bacteria grow.

4.q: What is the most common way contamination gets into a water main during work?
o: Through an open, unprotected pipe end
Straight through the solid pipe walls
By the water slowly evaporating away
Through a correctly fitted, sound valve
4.w: Open, unprotected pipe ends are the main route by which contamination enters a main.

n.1: Sound pipe walls do not let contamination through.
n.2: Evaporation does not introduce contamination.
n.3: A correctly fitted valve is not an entry point.

4.q: The bacteria that cause Weil's disease usually get into water through what?
o: Rainwater running off from a clean building roof
Chlorine dosed into the main to disinfect it
Contamination by the urine of rats and other rodents
Rust flaking away from old cast-iron pipework
4.w: Water becomes a risk when rats' or rodents' urine contaminates it.

n.0: Clean rainwater is not the source; rodent urine is.
n.1: Chlorine is a disinfectant, not a source of the disease.
n.3: Rust does not carry leptospira; contaminated urine does.

4.q: Ingress of contaminated water into a clean-water main is serious because it can:
o: Only affect the colour of the water for a short while
Introduce harmful bacteria into the public supply
Improve the disinfection of the whole network
Reduce the pressure but never affect water quality
4.w: Contaminated ingress can carry harmful bacteria into the drinking water supply, putting the public at risk.

n.0: It is a health risk, not just a brief colour change.
n.2: Ingress contaminates the supply rather than disinfecting it.
n.3: It affects water quality directly, not merely pressure.

4.q: Which is the correct combination of what water fittings law aims to prevent?
o: Noise, dust and vibration from the works
Overtime, delays and rising project costs
Contamination, waste and misuse of water
Traffic, parking and access to the site
4.w: The fittings regulations aim to prevent contamination, waste and misuse of water.

n.0: These are site nuisances, not what the fittings law targets.
n.1: These are commercial issues, not the law's aim.
n.3: These are site logistics, not the law's aim.

4.q: A bucket used to bail foul water from the trench should be:
o: kept away from clean pipe unless disinfected
used next to carry clean jointing water
stored away inside the open end of the new pipe
tipped out over the stored fittings
4.w: A foul-water bucket is contaminated, so it is kept from clean pipe unless it has been disinfected.

n.1: Using it for clean water spreads contamination.
n.2: Storing it in the pipe contaminates the bore.
n.3: Tipping it over fittings soils them.

4.q: Health screening questionnaires for water workers are mainly used to identify:
o: Those workers who would prefer either early or late shifts
Anyone who might pass an infection into the water supply
Which of the workers own and run their own private transport
Which worker happens to have the longest service at the depot
4.w: Screening is mainly to identify anyone who might pass an infection into the water.

n.0: Shift preference is not what health screening is for.
n.2: Transport is irrelevant to a health questionnaire.
n.3: Length of service is not the purpose of the screening.

4.q: If you are unsure whether a tool has been in foul water, the safe approach is to:
o: assume it is clean and use it
treat it as dirty and disinfect it
give it a quick shake and carry on
ask later and keep working now
4.w: When in doubt, the tool is treated as contaminated and disinfected before use on the clean main.

n.0: Assuming it is clean risks contaminating the water.
n.2: A shake does nothing to make it safe.
n.3: Working on while unsure risks contamination.

4.q: A contractor knowingly allows dirty water to enter a drinking main. Under the Water Industry Act 1991 this is best described as:
o: A criminal offence for which they may be prosecuted
A minor issue that is dealt with by a warning
A civil matter to be settled privately between the firms
An acceptable everyday risk on live networks
4.w: Contaminating water likely to be used for human consumption is a criminal offence under Section 70.

n.1: Contaminating drinking water is treated as a criminal offence, not simply a warning.
n.2: It is a criminal matter, not merely a private dispute between companies.
n.3: Allowing contamination is never an acceptable risk on a live drinking-water network.

4.q: Why is it not acceptable to plug an open end with rag or paper?
o: They are simply too expensive to use up on the works
They make the pipe far too heavy to lift
They happen to be the wrong colour code
They shed fibres and carry contamination in
4.w: Rag and paper are not clean, sealed caps; they shed fibres and can carry contamination.

n.0: Cost is not the issue.
n.1: Weight is not the concern.
n.2: Colour coding is irrelevant here.

4.q: The previous gang left a pipe end open overnight in a wet trench. The operative should:
o: Suspect contamination and not simply connect it
Connect it quickly in order to make up lost time
Assume the overnight water has cleaned it out
Ignore it, since it was not their own doing
4.w: A pipe left open overnight in water should be treated as contaminated, not simply connected.

n.1: Speed must not override hygiene.
n.2: Standing water contaminates, not cleans.
n.3: The risk must be dealt with regardless.

4.q: A new clean-water main should be kept well away from:
o: any other clean-water mains sited nearby
sewers, drains and other foul services
the marker tape that is laid above it
the clean bedding stone around the pipe
4.w: Separation from sewers and drains reduces the risk of foul contamination reaching the drinking-water main.

n.0: Clean-water mains are not a foul-contamination risk.
n.2: Marker tape is part of the clean-water works.
n.3: Bedding stone is clean material around the pipe.

4.q: On site you realise unclean water may have entered the main you are working on. Why is this urgent?
o: Because the unsafe water could reach and harm many consumers
Because the job will now take somewhat longer for the team to finish off
Because your tools may need a quick rinse afterwards
Because the paperwork will need an extra signature
4.w: It is urgent because unsafe water could harm many consumers.

n.1: A longer job is not why the situation is urgent.
n.2: Rinsing tools is not the urgent public-health issue.
n.3: Extra paperwork is not the urgent concern.

4.q: Which of these best describes why the ground itself is a source of contamination?
o: Soil is a fully certified, clean laid material
Soil disinfects any pipe that it happens to touch
Soil only ever contains completely harmless sand
Soil naturally holds bacteria and other organisms
4.w: Soil naturally contains bacteria and other micro-organisms, making the ground a source.

n.0: Soil is not certified clean; it holds organisms.
n.1: Soil contaminates rather than disinfects.
n.2: Soil holds organisms, not just sand.

4.q: Scenario: Your standpipe has no check valve fitted and none is available. What should you do?
o: Draw the water quickly before pressure has time to drop on the day
Fit any spare valve you can find, whatever its type that morning
Do not draw water until proper backflow protection is fitted
Keep a second operative ready to shut the hydrant fast to save time
4.w: Without correct backflow protection the main is at risk, so no water should be drawn.

n.0: A quick draw does not remove the backflow risk.
n.1: Only correct, approved protection should be used.
n.3: A quick shut-off does not replace a check valve.

4.q: If you are unsure how close a sewer is to your new main, you should:
o: Carry on and lay the main quickly before the sewer is exposed
Find out and take extra care to keep the main clear of the sewer
Assume there is plenty of room and keep the pipes side by side
Dig faster so that the two pipes spend less time open together
4.w: You find out the sewer's position and take extra care to keep the water main clear of it.

n.0: Rushing before you know the layout is unsafe.
n.2: Assuming there is room without checking is a gamble.
n.3: Digging faster does nothing to protect the main.

4.q: Pipe left lying directly on the ground overnight is a problem because:
o: it may fade in colour by the morning
dirt, water and vermin can get into it
it becomes too heavy to lift by hand
it will not fit the couplings any longer
4.w: Ground contact and open ends let soil, standing water and vermin contaminate the pipe.

n.0: Colour fading is not a hygiene risk.
n.2: Lying on the ground does not change the pipe's weight.
n.3: Ground storage does not alter the coupling size.

4.q: Good welfare facilities for water network operatives should include:
o: A generous supply of chilled and fizzy soft drinks only
A television set and a few comfortable padded armchairs
Clean water, soap and somewhere hygienic to eat
A securely locked cabinet for storing personal valuables
4.w: Welfare should include clean water, soap and a hygienic place to eat.

n.0: Welfare is about hand washing and clean eating, not just soft drinks.
n.1: Entertainment is not the purpose of welfare facilities.
n.3: Valuables storage is not the core purpose of welfare provision.

4.q: Why must the correct contact time be observed when chlorinating a main?
o: Because a longer wait always makes the water taste much better
The disinfectant needs time in contact with the pipe to work effectively
Because the pipe must cool down before it can be used again
Because the swab needs time to dissolve inside the main for the customer supplied by that main
4.w: Chlorine acts over time, so cutting the hold short can leave the main not properly disinfected.

n.0: Contact time is about disinfection, not improving taste.
n.2: There is no cooling step; the hold is for the chlorine to act.
n.3: The swab is recovered earlier; contact time concerns the chlorine hold.

4.q: A washer made of the wrong rubber can contaminate water by:
o: giving it an unpleasant taste or odour
making the tap harder to turn off
making the flow through it slightly faster
making the washer wear out sooner
4.w: The wrong rubber can taint water, giving an unpleasant taste or smell.

n.1: A stiffer tap is not the contamination effect.
n.2: Faster flow is not the contamination effect.
n.3: Faster wear is not the contamination effect.

4.q: Before heavily chlorinated water from disinfecting a main is discharged to a stream, it must be:
o: De-chlorinated or neutralised so the chlorine does not harm the watercourse
Warmed up so it matches the temperature of the stream water
Dyed a bright colour so people can see where it goes throughout the length of the new main
Left standing in the sun for several weeks before release
4.w: Super-chlorinated water is toxic to aquatic life, so the chlorine is neutralised before discharge.

n.1: Temperature is not the issue; the chlorine must be neutralised first.
n.2: Dyeing does not make the water safe to discharge; neutralising does.
n.3: Ad-hoc standing is not the controlled method; neutralising is required.

4.q: Which of the following would the Drinking Water Inspectorate be most interested in?
o: A delay in a company's monthly payroll
A report of unsafe or discoloured tap water
A dispute over the office parking spaces
A change to a firm's company logo
4.w: The DWI focuses on drinking water safety, so unsafe or discoloured water would concern it.

n.0: Payroll is not a drinking-water quality matter.
n.2: Parking disputes are nothing to do with the DWI.
n.3: Branding is not the DWI's concern.

4.q: An operative should treat every main that has been opened as:
o: Potentially contaminated until it has been disinfected and passed a sample
Automatically clean because the water inside looked clear
Ready for supply as soon as the pipe is rejoined at that stage of the disinfection work
Free of any risk because chlorine is already in the network
4.w: Assuming possible contamination until confirmed clean is the safe working approach.

n.1: Clear-looking water can still be contaminated; disinfection is required.
n.2: Rejoining the pipe does not make the water safe; disinfection is needed.
n.3: Network chlorine does not remove the need to disinfect an opened main.

4.q: Which of these best protects the inside of a new main?
o: Leaving both ends open to dry the bore out
Storing pipe with its ends in the mud
Rinsing out the bore with dirty trench water
Capping ends and keeping the bore clean
4.w: Capped ends and a clean bore keep contamination out of the inside of the main.

n.0: Open ends let dirt and vermin into the bore.
n.1: Ends in the mud contaminate the bore.
n.2: Trench water in the bore adds contamination.

5.q: A main is disinfected after being opened mainly to protect:
o: The colour of the customer's water at the kitchen tap
The value of the pipe material used in the repair once the pipe has been rejoined
The health of customers who will drink the water it supplies
The speed at which the trench can be backfilled again
5.w: Disinfection removes any contamination introduced so the water stays safe to drink.

n.0: Disinfection protects health, not the colour of the water.
n.1: Disinfection is about public health, not the pipe's value.
n.3: Backfill speed has nothing to do with why disinfection is done.

5.q: A stack of fittings has lost its protective caps. Before use you should:
o: fit them straight away without checking
clean and check each one for contamination
rinse them once or twice in the trench water
cap them again and fit them unchecked
5.w: Once caps are off, fittings may have picked up dirt, so each must be cleaned and checked before use.

n.0: Fitting uncapped items risks putting dirt in the main.
n.2: Trench water is dirty and would not clean them.
n.3: Re-capping without checking does not remove any dirt already in.

5.q: Which of the following is a recognised source of Weil's disease?
o: A clean, dry and well-heated site welfare cabin
Freshly chlorinated and flushed storage tanks
Sewers and other wet places frequented by rats
Sealed bottled drinking water from the shop
5.w: Sewers and rat-frequented wet places are a recognised source of the disease.

n.0: A clean site cabin is not a source of leptospirosis.
n.1: Chlorinated water is disinfected and not a source.
n.3: Sealed bottled water is not contaminated with rodent urine.

5.q: Which of these on site would you treat as a likely source of chemical contamination?
o: A sealed, unopened bottle of clean drinking water
A leaking can of fuel sat near the excavation
A bag of clean, certified pipe fittings
A length of new, capped plastic water pipe
5.w: A leaking fuel can beside the dig can introduce chemicals into the works.

n.0: A sealed bottle is not a source of contamination.
n.2: Clean certified fittings are not a chemical source.
n.3: New capped pipe is clean and protected.

5.q: The Weil's disease warning card is most useful at which moment?
o: When you become ill and need to see a doctor
When you very first apply for a job on the network
When you go to collect your weekly wages from the office
When you next go to renew your ordinary driving licence
5.w: It is most useful when you fall ill and need to see a doctor.

n.1: The card's value is at the point of illness, not at job application.
n.2: The card is a health alert, not a payslip.
n.3: The card has nothing to do with a driving licence.

5.q: Flushing after disinfection continues until the water leaving the main:
o: Turns a deep blue colour to show the chlorine is present once the pipe has been rejoined
No longer carries the high chlorine level used for the disinfection
Stops flowing altogether from the end of the length of main
Becomes noticeably warmer than when the flush first started
5.w: Flushing runs until the chlorine has been cleared to a normal supply level.

n.0: Chlorine does not turn the water blue; flushing lowers the chlorine.
n.2: Flushing needs flow to clear the chlorine; it does not run to a stop.
n.3: Flushing is judged by chlorine clearance, not by temperature.

5.q: During an audit, several operatives cannot produce a valid card. The correct action is that they:
o: keep working and sort the cards out later on
swap cards around so each person shows one
stop restricted work until a valid card is shown
carry on if the job is very nearly finished
5.w: Restricted work should stop until a valid card is produced.

n.0: Restricted work should not continue without a valid card.
n.1: Swapping cards is not acceptable or honest.
n.3: Being nearly finished does not allow uncarded work.

5.q: Why is a sudden loss of pressure during a burst a contamination concern?
o: Low pressure guarantees the main is now completely sterile
Low pressure has no real effect at all on what can get into an open pipe
Low or negative pressure can draw dirty water back into the main
Low pressure only affects the customer's taps and nothing else
5.w: When pressure falls or goes negative, external dirty water can be sucked back into the pipe through the break.

n.0: Low pressure does not sterilise the main.
n.1: Low pressure directly affects the risk of back-drawn contamination.
n.3: The effect reaches the main itself, not just customer taps.

5.q: A fitter spills two-stroke oil right next to an open pipe end. This is an example of which type of contamination?
o: Microbiological contamination from living organisms
Chemical contamination from the oil entering the works
Physical contamination from solid foreign matter and debris
Thermal contamination from the temperature change
5.w: Oils, fuels and solvents are chemicals, so this is chemical contamination.

n.0: That involves bacteria or viruses, not oil.
n.2: That means solids such as soil or debris.
n.3: Temperature is not one of the three types.

5.q: Why must jointing compounds be approved before use on mains water?
o: So they last longer on the shelf
So they cannot contaminate the water
So they are cheaper for us to buy in bulk
So they are easier to spread on
5.w: Approval ensures the compound will not contaminate the drinking water.

n.0: Shelf life is not why compounds must be approved.
n.2: Cost is not why compounds must be approved.
n.3: Ease of spreading is not why they must be approved.

5.q: An operative has left their valid card in another jacket at home. Best practice is that they:
o: bring a valid card before restricted work
carry on since they know they have passed
borrow a workmate's card just for the day
use last year's expired card for the shift
5.w: The valid card should be brought before restricted work.

n.1: Knowing you passed is not the same as carrying the card.
n.2: You cannot use someone else's card.
n.3: An expired card cannot be used for the work.

5.q: Why is it wrong to assume the mains pressure will always stop backflow on its own?
o: Mains pressure is measured only once when the pipe is first laid
Mains pressure is the same value in every pipe across the country
Mains pressure is set by the customer at their own stop tap
Mains pressure can drop or be exceeded, leaving the supply unprotected
5.w: Pressure is not guaranteed; it can fall or be overcome, so physical protection is still needed.

n.0: Pressure is not a one-off reading; it changes constantly in use.
n.1: Pressure varies by location and demand, not a single national value.
n.2: Customers do not set mains pressure; the network does.

5.q: The point of flushing before the sample is taken is to make sure the sample:
o: Contains as much chlorine as possible when it reaches the lab
Represents the water customers will actually receive, not the strong chlorine
Carries some of the debris the swab left behind in the pipe
Is taken from the coldest part of the length of new main at that stage of the disinfection work
5.w: Flushing first means the sample reflects normal supply water rather than disinfection strength.

n.0: The sample should reflect supply water, not maximum chlorine.
n.2: A good sample is clean, not carrying swab debris.
n.3: The sample reflects supply quality; the coldest point is not the aim.

5.q: Which best describes correct standpipe practice on a hydrant?
o: Use an approved standpipe with a double check valve every time
Use any spare standpipe as long as it fits the hydrant
Use a standpipe only when the main pressure is very low in practice
Use a standpipe without a valve for short jobs only
5.w: Correct practice is always to use an approved standpipe fitted with a double check valve.

n.1: Merely fitting the hydrant does not make a standpipe compliant.
n.2: Standpipes are not restricted to low-pressure conditions.
n.3: Even short jobs require the double check valve; there is no exemption.

5.q: Checking a product against an approved list mainly protects:
o: the tidiness of your paperwork
the quality and safety of the water
the amount of profit made on the job
the time taken to finish work
5.w: Checking approval protects the water's quality and safety for the public.

n.0: Paperwork tidiness is not the point of the check.
n.2: Profit is not the point of the check.
n.3: Saving time is not the point of the check.

5.q: Short scenario: the bore has a smear of mud near the end. Before jointing you should:
o: joint it and let water clear the mud
wipe over only the outside of that end
smear it around evenly so it is less obvious
clean the bore until it is free of mud
5.w: Mud in the bore is contamination, so it is cleaned out fully before the joint is made.

n.0: Relying on water to clear mud leaves contamination in.
n.1: The bore, not just the outside, must be clean.
n.2: Spreading the mud does not remove it.

5.q: The best way to keep the connection point clean while working is to:
o: Leave them open so any water can drain out freely
Keep couplings capped or covered when not connected
Rest them against the kerb to keep them off the van
Push a rag from your pocket into each open end on the day
5.w: Capping or covering open ends keeps dirt out of the connection point.

n.0: Open ends collect dirt and debris while uncovered.
n.2: The kerb is dirty and would contaminate the ends.
n.3: A pocket rag can introduce its own contamination.

5.q: If backflow introduces bacteria into the main, what may customers experience?
o: Sickness such as stomach upsets from drinking the water
A pleasant improvement in how the water tastes
A permanent increase in their available water pressure on site
A reduction in the hardness of the water supplied
5.w: Bacterial contamination can cause gastrointestinal illness among those who drink the affected water.

n.1: Contamination worsens, not improves, water quality.
n.2: There is no pressure benefit from contamination.
n.3: Backflow does not soften the water; it pollutes it.

5.q: Which of these is least likely to be a Restricted Operation?
o: swabbing the inside of a clean water main
fitting a new valve on the supply network
entering a clean water storage tank to work
mowing grass at a depot well away from mains
5.w: Mowing grass away from mains does not affect water quality.

n.0: Swabbing a main can affect water quality, so it is restricted.
n.1: Fitting a valve on the network is a restricted operation.
n.2: Entering a clean water tank is a restricted operation.

5.q: Why are end caps left on new pipe and fittings until they are fitted?
o: To make the whole pipe stack look tidy on the site
To stop the pipe rolling around the store
To keep the inside clean until the moment of use
To protect the paint on the outside surface
5.w: End caps stop dirt, insects and germs getting inside the pipe before it is jointed.

n.0: Tidiness is not the reason for keeping caps on.
n.1: Caps are about cleanliness inside, not stopping rolling.
n.3: The concern is the inside of the pipe, not outside paint.

5.q: Silicone or other grease used on a drinking water seal must be:
o: the thickest grease that you can find
any grease that is easy to apply
an approved food-grade or WRAS type
the same grease used on machinery
5.w: Only an approved grease suitable for drinking water may be used on the seal.

n.0: Thickness does not make a grease approved.
n.1: Ease of use does not make a grease approved.
n.3: Machinery grease is not approved for water.

5.q: Disinfection whenever a main is opened is part of the wider aim of:
o: Keeping the public clean water supply safe and free from contamination
Reducing the amount the water company spends on chlorine for the customer supplied by that main
Making sure the pipe is always exactly the same temperature
Ensuring every customer receives brightly coloured water
5.w: It protects the integrity of the drinking water network against contamination.

n.1: The aim is public health protection, not saving on chlorine.
n.2: Disinfection is a hygiene measure, unrelated to pipe temperature.
n.3: The aim is safe, uncontaminated water, not coloured water.

5.q: The reason strong chlorine is used to disinfect a main and then removed is that it:
o: Makes the pipe joints set harder the longer it is left in while the job is being carried out
Improves the colour of the water for the customer's benefit
Kills organisms during the hold but is too strong to leave in the supply
Increases the pressure the main can safely carry in service
5.w: Chlorine at disinfection strength deals with organisms but must be flushed before customers drink it.

n.0: Chlorine does not cure joints; it disinfects and is then flushed out.
n.1: Chlorine is used to disinfect, not to improve the water's colour.
n.3: Chlorine has no bearing on the main's pressure rating.

5.q: What is the main risk of using a dirty standpipe on the network?
o: Contamination can be introduced into the public water supply
The standpipe may become slightly harder to fit that morning
The hydrant chamber may fill up with rainwater for the shift
The water may come out at a lower flow rate if time is short
5.w: A dirty standpipe can carry contamination straight into the public supply.

n.1: A tight fit is a nuisance, not the real hazard here.
n.2: A wet chamber is not the contamination concern raised.
n.3: Flow rate is not the danger posed by a dirty standpipe.

5.q: Recommissioning is the stage where a repaired main is:
o: Cut open and exposed to the dirty trench for the first time
Left isolated and out of use for several weeks
Deliberately drained down and abandoned in place
Brought carefully back into normal service and supply
5.w: Recommissioning is the controlled process of bringing the repaired main back into normal service and supply.

n.0: Cutting open is part of the repair, not recommissioning.
n.1: Recommissioning brings the main back, it does not leave it idle.
n.2: The main is returned to service, not abandoned.

6.q: A new operative asks what water hygiene is really 'for'. The best reply is that it is for:
o: Keeping the storage yard tidy and organised
Keeping all of the digging equipment properly maintained
Keeping the paperwork up to date each week
Keeping the public's drinking water clean and safe
6.w: Water hygiene is for keeping the public's water clean and safe.

n.0: A tidy yard is not what water hygiene is for.
n.1: Equipment maintenance is not the aim of hygiene.
n.2: Paperwork upkeep is not the aim of hygiene.

6.q: When water is being pumped out of a trench, the discharge should be:
o: Aimed at the pipe ends to give them a final rinse before jointing
Left to soak into the trench floor a short distance from the pump
Directed well away so that it cannot run straight back into the dig
Sent into the open end of the new main to test it for any leaks
6.w: Discharge must be sent well clear so the same water cannot flow straight back into the excavation.

n.0: Trench discharge water must never be used to rinse pipe ends.
n.1: Letting it soak nearby lets it drain back into the trench.
n.3: Discharge water must never be put into the drinking main.

6.q: Even if a repaired main 'looks fine', it is still disinfected because:
o: Harmful bacteria and dirt cannot be seen but may have entered while it was open
Disinfection is only ever done to give the water a nicer taste
A repaired main must always be painted before it is reused while the job is being carried out
The chlorine is needed to glue the repair section into place
6.w: Contamination is invisible, so disinfection is done regardless of how the pipe looks.

n.1: Disinfection guards against invisible contamination, not to flavour water.
n.2: Painting is not part of returning a repaired main to supply.
n.3: Chlorine does not act as a glue; it deals with contamination.

6.q: What should you tell any doctor treating you if you work with water or sewage?
o: That you would honestly rather not have any tests done
That your work exposes you to water and sewage, so Weil's disease is possible
That you have never once felt unwell before this moment
That you only ever work indoors in a clean, dry office
6.w: Telling the doctor about water and sewage exposure helps them diagnose Weil's disease.

n.0: Withholding tests is unhelpful; you should flag the exposure risk.
n.2: Your past health is less important than flagging the exposure.
n.3: This would be untrue and would hide the real risk from the doctor.

6.q: Why is it important to report problems with hydrants and standpipes?
o: So faults are fixed before they can affect the supply
So the operative can claim extra pay for the day on the day
So the paperwork looks fuller at the week's end that morning
So the same hydrant is never opened again to save time
6.w: Prompt reporting means faults can be corrected before they harm the supply.

n.1: Reporting is about safety, not about extra pay.
n.2: Reporting is not done to pad out the paperwork.
n.3: Reporting does not mean a hydrant is closed forever.

6.q: The best reason to report a near miss that could have contaminated water is that it:
o: Guarantees the operative a cash bonus
Ends the need for any hygiene rules
Removes the need to record the work
Helps prevent a real contamination later
6.w: Reporting near misses helps prevent a genuine contamination event in the future.

n.0: Reporting is a duty, not a route to a bonus.
n.1: Hygiene rules remain necessary regardless.
n.2: Recording work is still required.

6.q: The National Water Hygiene scheme sits under which sector's skills register?
o: the energy and utilities sector register (EUSR)
the construction and civil engineering register
the transport and logistics skills register
the healthcare and clinical professionals register
6.w: It sits under the energy and utilities sector register, EUSR.

n.1: It is not under a construction sector register.
n.2: It is not under a transport sector register.
n.3: It is not under a healthcare register.

6.q: Which statement about prosecution under the Water Industry Act 1991 is correct?
o: Only foreign contractors can ever be prosecuted
Prosecution can never involve individual workers
Both individuals and companies can face prosecution
Only the Government itself can be prosecuted
6.w: The law allows both an individual and their employer to be prosecuted for a contamination offence.

n.0: Nationality is irrelevant; anyone can be prosecuted for the offence.
n.1: Individuals absolutely can be prosecuted, which is why personal responsibility matters.
n.3: The Government is not the target; workers and companies can be prosecuted.

6.q: The public water supply that you work on is required by law to be:
o: Softened so that it never leaves any limescale
Wholesome and safe for consumers to drink
Perfectly still with no dissolved oxygen at all
Free of every mineral that gives water its taste
6.w: Public supplies must legally be wholesome and safe to drink.

n.0: Softness is not a legal requirement for potability.
n.2: Dissolved oxygen does not stop water being potable.
n.3: Harmless taste-giving minerals are allowed in supplies.

6.q: The initials DWI stand for:
o: The Domestic Water Installers group
The Drinking Water Inspectorate
The District Waste Investigators unit
The Drainage Works Inspectorate body
6.w: DWI stands for the Drinking Water Inspectorate, the drinking water regulator.

n.0: This is not what DWI stands for in the water industry.
n.2: This is not the correct meaning of the initials DWI.
n.3: DWI refers to drinking water, not drainage works.

6.q: A colleague wants to borrow your saw that has been in dirty water. You should:
o: tell them it needs disinfecting first
hand it over as it looks clean enough
lend it but say to rinse it after
lend it only for cutting the spoil boards
6.w: The saw is contaminated, so it must be disinfected before anyone uses it on clean-water work.

n.1: Looking clean does not mean it is free of germs.
n.2: Rinsing afterwards does not undo contamination during use.
n.3: Any clean-water cutting risks carrying germs in.

6.q: 'Restricted Operations' are tasks that could:
o: affect the pressure recorded at a customer's tap
affect the cost of running the treatment works
affect the working hours of the on-site team
affect the quality of water in the public supply
6.w: Restricted Operations are tasks that could affect public water quality.

n.0: The definition is about water quality, not pressure alone.
n.1: The definition is about quality, not running costs.
n.2: The definition is about quality, not working hours.

6.q: Which is the correct order of reliability, strongest first, for common backflow protection?
o: Single check valve, then double check valve, then air gap
Double check valve, then air gap, then single check valve
Air gap, then double check valve, then single check valve
Single check valve, then air gap, then double check valve
6.w: An air gap is the most reliable, a double check valve next, and a single check valve suits only the lowest risk.

n.0: This reverses the order; a single check valve is the weakest.
n.1: An air gap outranks a double check valve, not the other way round.
n.3: A single check valve is the weakest and should not come first.

6.q: A supervisor pressures the team to reconnect a main quickly before it has been sampled. The right response is to:
o: Explain the sample must be taken before returning to supply
Reconnect at once and take the sample the following day
Reconnect but warn the customer to boil their water
Reconnect and hope the water quality turns out fine
6.w: The required sample must be taken before the main returns to supply, and the operative should say so rather than cut the step.

n.1: Reconnecting before sampling exposes consumers to any contamination.
n.2: A boil notice does not replace the required hygiene steps.
n.3: Hoping for the best is not an acceptable hygiene decision.

6.q: Why should surges and rapid pressure changes be avoided when recommissioning a main?
o: Because they can disturb deposits and discolour the water
Because they make the new joint permanently stronger
Because they are needed to force air out quickly
Because they help the sample pass more reliably
6.w: Surges stir up deposits in the pipe and can discolour the water, so pressure is changed gradually.

n.1: Surges do not strengthen the joint; they cause quality problems.
n.2: Air is vented gently, not forced out with surges.
n.3: Surges make discolouration more likely, not less.

6.q: Reporting a contamination concern promptly is important because it:
o: Reduces the operative's take-home wages
Helps to protect public health quickly
Slows down the whole of the project
Avoids having to do any paperwork
6.w: Prompt reporting lets action be taken quickly to protect people from unsafe water.

n.0: Reporting does not reduce wages.
n.2: Protecting health matters more than project speed, and reporting need not stall work.
n.3: Reporting usually involves recording, not avoiding, paperwork.

6.q: Plugs and caps used to close open ends should themselves be:
o: clean before they are put on the pipe
muddy so they grip the bore tightly
coated in oil to slide in easily
any old size that roughly fits
6.w: A dirty or oily plug would contaminate the very end it is meant to protect, so it must be clean.

n.1: Mud on a plug puts dirt straight into the bore.
n.2: Oil on a plug contaminates the clean-water surface.
