n.3: A poorly fitting plug leaves gaps for dirt to enter.

6.q: A low or zero residual chlorine after the contact time usually calls for:
o: Putting the main straight into supply to save time on the job
Adding more debris to the pipe to use up the spare chlorine for the customer supplied by that main
Reducing the contact time on the next main to match this one
Reviewing and, if needed, repeating the disinfection before the main is used
6.w: If the chlorine did not hold, the main may not be disinfected and the process is repeated.

n.0: A failed residual is not a reason to supply; it is a reason to redo the work.
n.1: Adding debris is never done; a failed residual means repeating disinfection.
n.2: A short residual does not justify cutting contact time elsewhere.

6.q: Why does contamination from one standpipe matter to the wider public?
o: Because each home has its own separate pipe network on the day
Because the standpipe belongs to a single property that morning
Because contamination stays inside the hose only to save time
The main is shared, so pollution can spread to many homes
6.w: Because the main is shared, contamination introduced at one point can reach many homes.

n.0: Homes share the same main, so this reasoning is wrong.
n.1: A standpipe on the main is not tied to one property.
n.2: Contamination can pass beyond the hose into the main.

6.q: Water hygiene practices are designed above all to protect:
o: The health of the public who drink the water
The paintwork on the outside of the network mains pipes
The speed at which the mains can be laid
The comfort of the operatives on site
6.w: Water hygiene exists chiefly to protect consumers' health.

n.1: Paintwork is not what water hygiene protects.
n.2: Laying speed is not the aim of water hygiene.
n.3: Operative comfort is not the purpose of water hygiene.

6.q: Which statement about the symptoms of Weil's disease is correct?
o: Early symptoms are flu-like and easily mistaken for a minor illness
The symptoms only ever appear within the first hour
It causes no symptoms whatsoever right up until death
The very first sign of it is always a broken bone
6.w: Its early symptoms are flu-like and can be mistaken for a minor illness.

n.1: Symptoms are not immediate; they develop over days and are flu-like at first.
n.2: It does cause symptoms, typically flu-like ones, before becoming severe.
n.3: Broken bones are not a symptom of the disease.

6.q: Beyond illness, what other consequence often follows a confirmed backflow contamination?
o: A do-not-drink or boil notice while the supply is made safe
An automatic discount applied to every customer bill
A permanent boost to the pressure across the district each time
A change of the water source to a completely new one
6.w: Customers may be told not to drink the water, or to boil it, until the supply has been flushed and confirmed safe.

n.1: Bill discounts are not the standard consequence of contamination.
n.2: There is no automatic pressure boost from an incident.
n.3: The source is not routinely swapped after a backflow event.

6.q: Extra separation between a water main and a sewer is required so that:
o: The two pipes do not rub together and wear each other away in time
Each pipe can be located separately with a signal tracer later on
The sewer can be dug up without disturbing the water main above it
A future sewer leak cannot contaminate the drinking-water main
6.w: Separation is required so that a future sewer leak cannot contaminate the drinking main.

n.0: Preventing wear is not the main reason for separation.
n.1: Tracing pipes separately is not why the gap is needed.
n.2: Ease of future digging is not the purpose of separation.

6.q: Which of these shows a failure to keep pipe ends protected?
o: Laying uncapped pipe overnight in an open trench
Fitting a clean plug to the end before a break
Capping both ends before the pipe is stored away
Keeping the plug on right up until connection
6.w: Leaving uncapped pipe overnight in the trench is a clear failure to protect the ends.

n.1: That is correct protection.
n.2: That is good practice.
n.3: That is the correct approach.

6.q: Which of these is a warning sign of possible contamination that should be reported?
o: Cool, clear water running at the correct pressure
Neatly bagged, clean and certified new fittings
A capped main sitting under steady, normal pressure
An unusual chemical or fuel smell in the trench
6.w: An unusual chemical or fuel smell suggests contamination and should be reported.

n.0: Normal clear water is not a warning sign.
n.1: Clean bagged fittings are not a hazard.
n.2: A capped main is well protected.

7.q: Why should hands be washed before drinking a cup of tea on a foul-contaminated site?
o: So that the mug is not left with dirty marks around its rim
So that the tea does not go cold while the hands are washed
So that the crew set a tidy example to the watching public
So that harmful germs are not swallowed along with the drink
7.w: Washing first stops germs on the hands being swallowed with the drink.

n.0: Marks on the mug are not the health issue.
n.1: The tea's temperature is not the reason to wash.
n.2: Setting an example is not the real purpose.

7.q: The main reason for de-watering the excavation before pipe-laying is to:
o: Make the trench sides easier to batter back to a safe angle
Reduce the weight the crew has to lift when backfilling later
Stop dirty or foul water getting into the new main during work
Allow the concrete surround to be poured a little more quickly
7.w: De-watering is done so that dirty or foul water cannot get into the new main during the work.

n.0: Battering the sides is a separate stability matter.
n.1: Backfill weight is not the reason for de-watering.
n.3: Speeding the concrete is not the purpose of keeping the trench dry.

7.q: Which decision on a repair job best protects public health?
o: Returning to supply before flushing to save time
Rinsing fittings in trench water to speed things up
Leaving open pipe ends uncapped between shifts
Refusing to return the main until it has passed its checks
7.w: Holding the main off supply until it passes its flushing, disinfection and any sample is the decision that protects the public.

n.0: Returning before flushing can send contaminated water to consumers.
n.1: Trench water contaminates fittings rather than cleaning them.
n.2: Uncapped ends let contamination into the main.

7.q: Why must a water main be disinfected whenever it has been opened for repair?
o: Because opening the main always makes the water flow the wrong way at that stage of the disinfection work
Because the customer will otherwise be charged too little for water
Because opening the main could have let in dirt or bacteria that must be removed
Because the pipe will not fit back together without chlorine added
7.w: Any opening risks contamination entering, so disinfection restores the water to a safe standard.

n.0: Disinfection deals with possible contamination, not the direction of flow.
n.1: Disinfection is a hygiene requirement, not a matter of billing.
n.3: Chlorine does not help the pipe fit; it deals with contamination.

7.q: Why should a water or sewage worker carry a Weil's disease warning card?
o: So they are able to claim extra money for doing wet work
So a doctor knows they work with water and may have Weil's disease
So that they are permitted onto the worksite each morning
So they can jump ahead of others in the doctor's queue
7.w: The card alerts a doctor to the water-work exposure so Weil's disease is considered.

n.0: The card is a medical warning, not a pay document.
n.2: The card is not a site access pass.
n.3: The card is to inform diagnosis, not to jump queues.

7.q: What is a standpipe used for on the clean water network?
o: To connect safely to a hydrant so water can be drawn from the main
To measure the chlorine level in the water at the tap that morning
To store several hours of drinking water on the vehicle on the day
To seal off a burst section of pipe during a repair during the job
7.w: A standpipe is the fitting that lets an authorised user connect to a hydrant and draw water.

n.1: A standpipe is a connector, not a water-quality measuring device.
n.2: Storage is done in a bowser or tank, not in the standpipe itself.
n.3: A burst is isolated with valves, not with a standpipe.

7.q: Which situation puts a new water main most at risk of foul contamination?
o: Laying it in a clean, separated trench
Laying it on a clean, de-watered bed
Laying it right beside a leaking sewer
Laying it with proper marker tape above
7.w: A leaking sewer alongside the main is a direct route for foul contamination.

n.0: A clean, separated trench is the safe way to lay it.
n.1: A clean, de-watered bed keeps the main protected.
n.3: Marker tape is part of good, safe practice.

7.q: Back-siphonage and back-pressure are the two types of backflow. What sets back-siphonage apart?
o: It is driven by high pressure downstream pushing water backwards
It only happens inside sealed tanks that hold no air at all
It is driven by low pressure in the supply pulling water backwards
It only happens when a pump is deliberately run in reverse
7.w: Back-siphonage is the low-pressure (suction) type; back-pressure is the opposite, high-pressure type.

n.0: High downstream pressure pushing water back is back-pressure, not siphonage.
n.1: Siphonage is not limited to sealed airless tanks.
n.3: A reversed pump is not required for siphonage to occur.

7.q: Giardiasis is caused by:
o: A protozoan parasite found in contaminated water
A bacterium closely related to typhoid
A virus that is very similar to the one causing hepatitis
A chemical that leaches from copper pipes
7.w: Giardiasis is caused by the protozoan parasite Giardia.

n.1: Giardiasis is protozoan, not a typhoid bacterium.
n.2: Giardiasis is not caused by a virus.
n.3: Giardiasis is a parasite, not a chemical.

7.q: A worker lights a cigarette while standing in a trench. Why is this poor hygiene practice?
o: Contaminants on the hands can pass to the mouth via the cigarette
The cigarette smoke will discolour the brand-new pipework
Cigarettes of any kind are banned on every outdoor worksite
It will make the trench far too warm and stuffy to work in
7.w: Handling a cigarette can carry contaminants from the hands into the mouth.

n.1: The rule is about the worker's health, not staining pipe.
n.2: The specific issue is hand-to-mouth contamination in the trench.
n.3: A cigarette does not overheat a trench; the risk is contamination.

7.q: A hiring agency phones to verify a candidate's water hygiene status. They should be directed to:
o: the candidate's previous training college
the card manufacturer's customer sales line
the site's own visitor sign-in book records
the EUSR register with the card details
7.w: The EUSR register holds card details for verification.

n.0: A former college does not verify current card status.
n.1: The card maker does not verify registration.
n.2: A visitor book does not verify water hygiene status.

7.q: The core reason we guard against backflow on potable networks is to protect what?
o: The quality and safety of the drinking water reaching the public
The flow rate available at the very end of a long main
The paint and coating on the inside of the water pipes
The record of how much water each customer has drawn
7.w: Backflow protection exists to keep the drinking water safe and clean for everyone on the supply.

n.1: Flow rate at the main's end is a supply issue, not the safety reason.
n.2: Pipe coatings are a durability matter, not the reason for backflow control.
n.3: Metering records are unrelated to preventing contamination.

7.q: The main reason certain water tasks are 'restricted' is to:
o: reduce the amount of paperwork done on site
limit how many firms can bid for the work
make the jobs take a bit longer to finish
keep the public drinking water safe to use
7.w: Tasks are restricted to keep drinking water safe.

n.0: Restriction is about safety, not paperwork.
n.1: Restriction is not about limiting bidders.
n.2: Restriction is not intended to slow jobs down.

7.q: On a job you notice a foul smell and signs that a nearby sewer may be leaking close to your open trench. Your main concern for the water main should be:
o: The strong smell simply making the job unpleasant to work in for you
The extra time needed to backfill the trench
Sewage getting into the main and contaminating the supply
The trench walls possibly collapsing inwards
7.w: The concern is sewage entering and contaminating the main.

n.0: An unpleasant smell is not the main hygiene concern.
n.1: Backfill time is not the contamination concern.
n.3: Trench collapse is a safety issue, not the hygiene risk.

7.q: A double check valve protects the public main by:
o: Letting water pass freely in both directions at once on the day
Closing completely and stopping all flow through it that morning
Allowing water out but blocking any flow back the other way
Adding chlorine automatically as the water leaves to save time
7.w: It permits forward flow to the hose but blocks reverse flow into the main.

n.0: Free flow both ways is exactly what the valve prevents.
n.1: A closed valve would stop the job, not protect the main.
n.3: The valve does not dose chemicals into the water.

7.q: Why are protozoa such as Cryptosporidium grouped with microbiological contamination?
o: They are living organisms that can cause illness
They are a type of dissolved chemical pollutant
They are small pieces of physical grit and sand
They are only ever found inside sealed clean pipe
7.w: Protozoa are micro-organisms, so they sit in the microbiological group with bacteria and viruses.

n.1: Protozoa are organisms, not chemicals.
n.2: They are microscopic organisms, not debris.
n.3: They come from soil and foul water.

7.q: Approved sealants for drinking water are formulated so that they do not:
o: taint the water or feed bacteria
set hard within a few minutes
come in either tubes or cartridges
need any cleaning before use
7.w: Approved sealants are made not to taint water or provide nutrients for bacteria.

n.1: Set time is not what approval is about.
n.2: Packaging is not what approval is about.
n.3: Cleaning before use is not what approval is about.

7.q: A worker off sick with flu-like symptoms sees their GP but does not mention their job. Why is that a problem?
o: The doctor will then refuse to see the worker at all
The worker will automatically lose their job on the network
The GP will immediately send the worker straight back to work
The doctor may not think to test for Weil's disease
7.w: Without knowing the job, the doctor may not test for Weil's disease.

n.0: The doctor will still see them; the risk is a missed diagnosis.
n.1: Not mentioning the job does not cost them their job; it risks their health.
n.2: The concern is a missed diagnosis, not being sent back to work.

7.q: Potable water is intended primarily for:
o: Flushing out sewers and clearing blocked public drains
Filling ornamental lakes and large public boating ponds
Cooling machinery inside factories and power stations
Drinking, cooking and other domestic uses by the public
7.w: Potable water is supplied for drinking, cooking and domestic use.

n.0: Sewer flushing does not require potable-quality water.
n.1: Ornamental water bodies do not need potable water.
n.2: Industrial cooling does not need drinking-quality water.

7.q: An operative gets foul water on a cut on their hand. They should:
o: Ignore it as small cuts tend to heal quickly enough on their own
Cover it with tape and keep working without washing it first
Rinse it in the trench water and just carry on with the task
Wash it well, cover it, and report it if it is at all serious
7.w: The cut is washed well, covered, and reported if serious, because foul water on broken skin is a real risk.

n.0: Ignoring foul water on a cut risks a serious infection.
n.1: Covering without washing traps contamination in the wound.
n.2: Trench water is contaminated and would make it worse.

7.q: The safest way to avoid contaminating the supply through a standpipe is to:
o: Work as fast as possible to limit exposure time on the day
Use clean, approved equipment exactly as authorised
Only draw water during the early morning hours that morning
Keep the tank lid off so you can watch the level to save time
7.w: Clean, approved equipment used as authorised is the reliable way to protect the supply.

n.0: Speed does not make dirty or unauthorised use safe.
n.2: Time of day does not reduce contamination risk.
n.3: An open lid can let contamination in, not keep it out.

7.q: Which of these is an offence under the Water Industry Act 1991?
o: Filling out a required hygiene record
Attending a routine safety toolbox talk
Wearing clean overalls to do the work
Wasting treated public water without cause
7.w: Wasting public water without justification is an offence under the Act.

n.0: Recording hygiene is good practice, not an offence.
n.1: Attending safety talks is expected, not an offence.
n.2: Clean overalls support hygiene and are not an offence.

7.q: 'Wholesome' water is best summarised as water that is:
o: Clean, safe and does not harm the health of consumers
Rich in extra minerals added deliberately for flavour
Sourced only from deep boreholes rather than rivers
Guaranteed to stay fresh for years once it is bottled
7.w: Wholesome water is clean, safe and harmless to health.

n.1: Wholesome water is not defined by added flavour minerals.
n.2: Wholesomeness does not depend on the type of source.
n.3: Long shelf life is not part of the meaning of wholesome.

7.q: Hepatitis A is best described as a waterborne disease that is:
o: A bacterial infection that is caught from the bites of insects
A viral infection spread by the faecal–oral route
A fungal infection picked up from damp soil
A parasite that lives only in warm sea water
7.w: Hepatitis A is a virus spread by the faecal–oral route.

n.0: Hepatitis A is viral and not insect-borne.
n.2: Hepatitis A is not a fungal soil infection.
n.3: Hepatitis A is a virus, not a sea-water parasite.

7.q: Why is it important to wash your hands even if you have worn gloves all shift?
o: Gloves make the hands smell far too strongly of rubber
Washing hands is only ever needed by the site office staff
Organisms can still reach the skin, so washing is essential
Gloves are far too costly to keep taking off and putting on
7.w: Organisms can still reach the skin under or around gloves, so washing is essential.

n.0: The reason is hygiene against organisms, not any rubber smell.
n.1: Hand washing applies to everyone doing the work, not just office staff.
n.3: Cost is not the reason; the hands still need washing for hygiene.

8.q: Fittings on site are lying uncovered in the dirt. The operative should recognise that they:
o: Are fine to fit as they are, since they are dry
Only need a quick shake to get them ready to use
Are contaminated and must be cleaned or replaced
Cannot possibly be contaminated out on the site
8.w: Fittings left in the dirt are contaminated and must be cleaned, swabbed or replaced before use.

n.0: Being dry does not make them clean.
n.1: A shake does not remove contamination.
n.3: Uncovered fittings in dirt are contaminated.

8.q: A hose end that has been lying in a tank of stored water should be treated as:
o: Perfectly clean because the tank holds water too on the day
Ready to use once it has simply dried off if time is short
Possibly contaminated and cleaned before it is used again
Safe as long as the tank looked clear inside that morning
8.w: Contact with stored tank water may contaminate the end, so it must be cleaned first.

n.0: Stored tank water is not necessarily clean or fresh.
n.1: Drying does not remove contamination from the end.
n.3: A clear look does not prove the water is uncontaminated.

8.q: Which of these correctly names the two types of backflow?
o: Back-siphonage and back-pressure
Back-siphonage and water hammer on site
Back-pressure and air-locking
Water hammer and stagnation
8.w: The two types of backflow are back-siphonage (low pressure) and back-pressure (high downstream pressure).

n.1: Water hammer is a surge, not a type of backflow.
n.2: Air-locking is a flow nuisance, not a type of backflow.
n.3: Neither water hammer nor stagnation is a type of backflow.

8.q: If an operative breaks the fittings regulations by using unapproved parts, the likely concern is that they may:
o: Finish the whole job far too quickly
Save the company far too much money
Cause contamination of the water supply
Use up too much of the clean water
8.w: Unapproved parts risk contaminating the supply, which the regulations aim to prevent.

n.0: Speed is not the concern with unapproved parts.
n.1: Saving money is not the risk; contamination is.
n.3: The main risk is contamination, not water use.

8.q: What long-term consequence can follow repeated poor backflow control on a site?
o: A steady fall in the water pressure across the county in everyday operation
Loss of trust and possible enforcement action against those responsible
A gradual improvement in the taste of the local water
A reduction in the number of pipes needed on site
8.w: Persistent failures can lead to enforcement and damage the reputation and standing of those responsible.

n.0: County-wide pressure decline is not a consequence of site failures.
n.2: Poor control worsens, not improves, water quality.
n.3: It does not reduce the pipework a site requires.

8.q: Which of these diseases can be spread through contaminated drinking water?
o: Measles
Malaria
Dysentery
Shingles
8.w: Dysentery is a waterborne disease linked to sewage-contaminated water.

n.0: Measles is spread through the air, not water.
n.1: Malaria is spread by mosquitoes, not drinking water.
n.3: Shingles is a reactivation of a virus, not waterborne.

8.q: Contamination gets into fittings before installation most often when they are:
o: Kept sealed inside their own packaging
Stored clean and up off the ground level
Left lying uncovered on the dirty ground
Swabbed over just before they are fitted
8.w: Fittings left uncovered on the ground pick up contamination before they are even installed.

n.0: Sealed fittings stay clean.
n.1: Clean raised storage protects them.
n.3: Swabbing keeps them clean.

8.q: Flushing a repaired main before returning it to supply is done to:
o: Fill the main slowly to avoid any air being trapped only
Raise the water pressure permanently across the district
Wash out any remaining dirt, debris and disinfectant
Warm the water so samples are easier to collect
8.w: Flushing runs water through at a good rate to wash out remaining dirt, debris and any disinfectant used.

n.0: Careful filling matters, but flushing is chiefly about washing the main out.
n.1: Flushing does not permanently raise district pressure.
n.3: Flushing is not about warming the water for sampling.

8.q: A task counts as a Restricted Operation when it could:
o: affect the general appearance of the work site
affect the delivery time of site materials
affect the quality of the public water supply
affect the noise levels near nearby homes
8.w: A task is restricted when it could affect public water quality.

n.0: Restriction is about water quality, not appearance.
n.1: Restriction is about water quality, not deliveries.
n.3: Restriction is about water quality, not noise.

8.q: The single most important personal-hygiene rule after touching foul material is to:
o: Change your gloves for a fresh pair before the next task begins
Rinse your face with any water that happens to be close to hand
Wash your hands well before you eat, drink or smoke anything
Finish the job first and leave all of the washing until you get home
8.w: Washing hands before eating, drinking or smoking is the key rule after foul contact.

n.0: Fresh gloves help but do not replace washing your hands.
n.1: Rinsing with any nearby water may add more contamination.
n.3: Leaving washing until home lets germs reach your mouth first.

8.q: Which of these correctly describes safe hose use when filling from the mains?
o: The outlet is pushed under the water to reduce splashing
The outlet is left in the water once filling has started
The outlet is held under the surface to stop it whipping
The outlet stays above the water leaving an air gap
8.w: Keeping the outlet above the water preserves an air gap, so nothing can be siphoned back.

n.0: Pushing it under the water creates the very risk to be avoided.
n.1: Leaving it submerged once started is still unsafe.
n.2: Holding it under the surface still submerges it.

8.q: De-chlorinating flush water before discharge is done to protect:
o: The colour of the water so it matches the local river
The pressure inside the main once it is put into supply
The taste of the water for customers at their taps before the main is put back into use
Fish, wildlife and the wider environment from the strong chlorine
8.w: Neutralising the chlorine safeguards aquatic life and the surrounding environment.

n.0: De-chlorination protects wildlife, not the water's appearance.
n.1: Neutralising discharge water has nothing to do with main pressure.
n.2: De-chlorination concerns safe disposal, not customer taste.

8.q: Besides after an illness, when might an employer ask a worker to complete a health questionnaire?
o: After buying themselves a new pair of work boots
After successfully passing their annual work appraisal
After certain kinds of foreign travel
After moving house to a completely new home address
8.w: Screening may be required after certain foreign travel as well as after illness.

n.0: New boots have nothing to do with health screening.
n.1: An appraisal is not the trigger for a health questionnaire.
n.3: A change of address does not trigger health screening.

8.q: What makes drinking-water contamination especially hard for the public to protect themselves against?
o: The water usually turns a very obvious, noticeable green colour
The water always froths up strongly in the glass
The water can look, smell and taste completely normal
The water becomes far too hot for anyone to drink safely
8.w: Contaminated water can appear normal, so people cannot tell.

n.0: Contaminated water is usually not obviously coloured.
n.1: Frothing is not a reliable sign of contamination.
n.3: Temperature is not how people detect contamination.

8.q: A bird has been getting into an unsealed hydrant chamber. This is a source of:
o: Chemical contamination from the bird's own feathers
Physical contamination only, with no risk
No contamination that is worth noting here
Microbiological contamination from droppings
8.w: Bird droppings carry micro-organisms, so an accessible chamber is a microbiological source.

n.0: Feathers are not a chemical hazard.
n.1: The droppings carry organisms, a real risk.
n.2: Animal access is a genuine risk.

8.q: After finishing with a standpipe, what should the operative do with it?
o: Clean it and return it to its proper storage
Leave it beside the hydrant for the next crew
Throw it in the back of the van still muddy
Give it to a passer-by who asks about it on the day
8.w: Cleaning and returning it to proper storage keeps it hygienic and controlled.

n.1: Leaving it out exposes it to dirt and possible misuse.
n.2: Storing it muddy lets contamination build up on it.
n.3: Handing kit to the public risks unauthorised use.

8.q: On a repair, keeping fittings capped, hands clean and the trench de-watered are all examples of:
o: Steps that can be skipped if the job is running late
Optional extras only needed on brand-new mains
Everyday hygiene precautions that protect the water supply
Measures required only when a sample is being taken
8.w: These are routine hygiene precautions that together protect the drinking water supply during any repair.

n.0: Hygiene steps are not skipped for time pressure.
n.1: They apply to repairs as well as new mains.
n.3: They are needed throughout, not only at sampling.

8.q: Which question best helps you decide if a fitting can go on a potable main?
o: Is it the cheapest fitting available today?
Is it the same colour as the pipe run?
Is it approved for contact with drinking water?
Is it made by a big and well-known company name?
8.w: Whether it is approved for drinking water is the question that decides its use.

n.0: Price does not decide whether a fitting is suitable.
n.1: Colour does not decide whether a fitting is suitable.
n.3: The maker does not decide whether it is suitable.

8.q: Why is hand washing before eating so important for a water worker?
o: It gently warms your cold hands up ready for your meal
It stops organisms on your hands being swallowed with your food
It takes away the lingering rubbery taste of your gloves
It helps make your rest break last a good deal longer
8.w: Washing removes organisms so they are not swallowed with food.

n.0: The purpose is hygiene, not warming your hands.
n.2: Washing is about removing organisms, not taste.
n.3: Hand washing is a health measure, not a way to extend breaks.

8.q: Which best explains why faecal matter is called the 'main' microbiological risk to drinking water?
o: It is the source of most disease-causing organisms in water
It is the only substance that ever discolours water
It is the heaviest material that can enter a pipe
It is the easiest contaminant for people to taste
8.w: Faecal matter supplies most of the pathogens found in water.

n.1: Faecal matter is not the only cause of discolouration.
n.2: Weight is irrelevant to why it is the main germ risk.
n.3: Faecal contamination is often undetectable by taste.

8.q: A pipe end briefly dipped into muddy trench water before being capped. You should treat the section as:
o: Perfectly clean, because the contact was only very brief
Improved, because the mud will seal small gaps in the joint
Contaminated, needing cleaning and disinfection before use
Unaffected, as trench water is the same as tap water
8.w: Even brief contact with muddy water contaminates the interior, so the section is cleaned and disinfected before use.

n.0: Brief contact is still enough to contaminate the pipe.
n.1: Mud does not seal joints; it contaminates the supply.
n.3: Trench water is dirty and is not equivalent to tap water.

8.q: Scenario: on a new main the swab is fired through but no debris comes out. The operative should:
o: Assume the pipe is unsafe and immediately abandon the whole main
Record the result and continue with the disinfection procedure as planned
Skip disinfection because a clean swab proves the water is safe according to the operative on site
Send the swab through many more times until debris finally appears
8.w: A clean swab run is a good sign; the process still moves on to chlorination.

n.0: A clean swab run does not condemn the main; the work continues.
n.2: Swabbing does not confirm safety; disinfection and sampling still follow.
n.3: Repeating pointlessly is not required; a clean run is recorded and work continues.

8.q: Which statement about waterborne diseases is correct?
o: They are all caused by the water being too hard
Many are spread when sewage contaminates drinking water
They are only ever caught from swimming pools
They come mainly from breathing in water vapour
8.w: Waterborne diseases largely spread via sewage in drinking water.

n.0: Hard water does not cause waterborne disease.
n.2: They are not limited to swimming pools.
n.3: Most are ingested, not breathed in as vapour.

8.q: Which statement about check valves is correct?
o: They let water pass equally in both directions at all times each time
They filter out any dirt carried in the flowing water
They add chlorine to the water as it passes through
They are designed to let water pass one way and stop it returning
8.w: A check valve allows forward flow but closes to prevent water travelling back, guarding against backflow.

n.0: A check valve is directional; it does not pass water both ways freely.
n.1: A check valve is not a filter.
n.2: A check valve does not dose chlorine.

8.q: Besides contamination, the Water Industry Act 1991 also creates offences relating to which of the following?
o: Charging customers an incorrect water tariff
Wasting or misusing public water supplies
Building new homes without planning consent
Failing to insure the company's work vehicles
8.w: The Act covers waste and misuse of water as well as contamination of drinking supplies.

n.0: Billing tariffs are not the water-protection offences you are taught under this Act.
n.2: Planning permission is a separate matter and not part of these water offences.
n.3: Vehicle insurance has nothing to do with the water offences in this Act.

9.q: The reason approved products are tested before approval is to check they do not:
o: cost more than rival products do
come in unusual sizes or shapes
release harmful substances into water
take far too long to be delivered to site
9.w: Approval testing confirms products will not release harmful substances into water.

n.0: Cost is not what approval testing checks.
n.1: Size or shape is not what approval testing checks.
n.3: Delivery time is not what approval testing checks.

9.q: It is raining hard and the trench keeps filling. The correct practical decision is to:
o: Keep pumping and protect the open ends from the water
Ignore the rain and joint the pipe under the water
Speed up and skip disinfection to beat the weather
Leave the job wide open and return only when the weather has cleared
9.w: You keep the excavation de-watered and the open ends protected so the wet conditions do not contaminate the main.

n.1: Jointing under water lets contamination into the pipe.
n.2: Skipping disinfection to save time compromises the supply.
n.3: Leaving an open main exposed invites further contamination.

9.q: A worker returns from a holiday abroad after a stomach illness there. What is a likely requirement?
o: Simply signing in at the site reception desk as normal
Bringing back a small souvenir for the rest of the depot
Completing a health questionnaire before returning to the network
Working a full week of night shifts in order to readjust
9.w: Illness abroad often means completing a health questionnaire before restricted work.

n.0: Signing in is not the same as the health screening this situation needs.
n.1: A souvenir has nothing to do with returning safely to water work.
n.3: Night shifts are not the health-clearance step required here.

9.q: Neutralising chlorinated water before discharge is an example of an operative:
o: Saving chlorine so it can be used again on the next main before the main is put back into use
Speeding the job up by skipping the disposal stage altogether
Protecting the environment as part of doing the disinfection job properly
Making the water stronger so it lasts longer in the main
9.w: Safe disposal of the flush water is part of the responsible completion of the work.

n.0: Neutralising destroys the chlorine's activity; it is not saved for reuse.
n.1: Neutralising is a required step, not something skipped to save time.
n.3: Neutralising weakens the chlorine and concerns disposal, not the main.

9.q: A bacteriological sample from a repaired main fails. The correct action is to:
o: Keep the main off supply and re-clean, flush and re-sample
Put the main straight into supply since one fail is normal
Ignore the result because the water looked perfectly clear
Take no further action until a customer complains of illness
9.w: A failed sample means the main is not safe, so it stays off supply and is re-treated and re-sampled until it passes.

n.1: A failed sample must not be overridden and put into supply.
n.2: Clear-looking water can still fail bacteriologically.
n.3: Action is needed at once, not only after illness is reported.

9.q: Keeping an excavation 'de-watered' on a clean-water job means:
o: Adding clean water to settle the dust at the bottom of the trench
Leaving rainwater in place to keep the pipe bedding nicely damp
Filling the trench with fresh water before the new pipe is laid
Removing standing and incoming water so the trench stays dry
9.w: De-watering means removing standing and incoming water so the excavation is kept dry.

n.0: Adding water is the opposite of de-watering.
n.1: Leaving rainwater in the trench is not de-watering.
n.2: Filling the trench with water is the reverse of keeping it dry.

9.q: Restricted Operations are controlled because water quality problems can:
o: only ever affect the operative doing the work
always be seen straight away by the naked eye
reach many customers on the network
be fixed simply by boiling water at the tap
9.w: Contamination can spread to many customers through the network.

n.0: Problems affect customers, not just the operative.
n.1: Contamination is often not visible to the eye.
n.3: Boiling does not remove all contamination risk.

9.q: Why keep fittings in their packaging until needed?
o: The wrapping stops them being counted
The wrapping makes them heavier to handle
The wrapping keeps them clean until fitting
The wrapping keeps them warm in cold weather
9.w: Original packaging protects fittings from dirt and germs right up to the point of use.

n.0: Packaging does not prevent stock being counted.
n.1: Weight is not the reason for keeping wrapping on.
n.3: Keeping fittings warm is not the hygiene purpose.

9.q: Soil, stones, grit and metal swarf getting into a main are examples of which type of contamination?
o: Chemical contamination from fuels and solvents
Microbiological contamination from organisms
Thermal contamination from a sudden change in heat
Physical contamination from solid foreign matter
9.w: Solid foreign matter such as soil, stones and swarf is classed as physical contamination.

n.0: That means substances such as fuel or solvents.
n.1: That means living organisms such as bacteria.
n.2: Temperature is not a recognised type.

9.q: After the registration period ends, continued restricted work requires the operative to:
o: complete a first aid course as a replacement
gain two more years of network experience
pass the water hygiene assessment once more
simply be signed off by their line manager
9.w: Continued work needs the assessment to be passed again.

n.0: A first aid course does not renew registration.
n.1: Extra experience does not renew registration.
n.3: A manager sign-off does not renew registration.

9.q: Why is ordinary multi-purpose grease unsuitable for drinking water fittings?
o: It can leach substances into the water
It is usually a dark grey colour
It can be a little too messy to use here
It costs more than approved grease
9.w: Ordinary grease can leach substances that contaminate the drinking water.

n.1: Its colour is not why it is unsuitable.
n.2: Being messy is not why it is unsuitable.
n.3: Cost is not why it is unsuitable.

9.q: An approved standpipe differs from an unapproved one mainly because it:
o: Includes the correct backflow protection to guard the main
Is always made from a brighter coloured metal that morning
Is a few centimetres longer than the older type on the day
Comes supplied with its own dedicated carry bag to save time
9.w: Approval centres on having the correct backflow protection fitted.

n.1: Colour is not what makes a standpipe approved.
n.2: Length is not the defining feature of an approved standpipe.
n.3: A carry bag has nothing to do with approval.

9.q: Holding a valid Blue Card mainly shows that the operative:
o: understands how to protect public water quality
is qualified to design new water treatment works
may carry out gas work on domestic properties
has completed a full plumbing apprenticeship scheme
9.w: The Blue Card shows the holder understands how to work without harming water quality.

n.1: The card shows hygiene awareness, not competence to design treatment works.
n.2: The card covers water hygiene, not gas work of any kind.
n.3: The card is not a plumbing apprenticeship qualification.

9.q: Approved jointing products are chosen so the finished joint is:
o: brightly coloured for later inspection
the cheapest possible joint to make
quick to take apart again later on
watertight and safe for drinking water
9.w: Approved products give a watertight joint that is safe for drinking water.

n.0: Colour is not the aim of an approved joint.
n.1: Being cheapest is not the aim of an approved joint.
n.2: Being easy to dismantle is not the aim.

9.q: The safest rule about grease and oil on potable water systems is:
o: use only lubricants approved for drinking water
use whatever grease keeps the joint moving
use the cheapest lubricant to save money
use a little of whatever oil happens to be handy
9.w: Only lubricants approved for drinking water should ever be used on the supply.

n.1: Keeping a joint moving does not justify unapproved grease.
n.2: Saving money does not justify unapproved lubricant.
n.3: Convenience does not justify unapproved oil.

9.q: Why do standpipes need particularly careful backflow protection?
o: They are always connected to sealed indoor plumbing only during the task
They are used in uncontrolled places where contamination is likely
They draw water far more slowly than any indoor tap
They are only ever used to fill sealed drinking bottles
9.w: Standpipes are used on sites and in the field where hoses may reach dirty water, so strong protection is essential.

n.0: Standpipes are used outdoors in uncontrolled settings, not just indoors.
n.2: Draw rate is not the reason they need protection.
n.3: Standpipes are used for many purposes, not only clean bottles.

9.q: A supervisor tells an operative to skip a hygiene step to save time. The operative should:
o: Obey the instruction without any question
Raise the concern and keep to the safe method
Skip two steps in order to catch up
Say nothing and just skip it quietly
9.w: The operative should raise the concern and continue working the safe, legal way.

n.0: Following an unsafe instruction can breach the law and risk water quality.
n.2: Skipping more steps increases the contamination risk.
n.3: Silently skipping hygiene breaches personal responsibility.

9.q: Stomach infections such as gastroenteritis can be caught on a water job by:
o: Swallowing germs after handling sewage-contaminated foul material
Standing near the running excavator for too long during the day
Wearing gloves that are slightly too large for the operative's hands
Looking directly at a freshly welded joint on the new water main
9.w: Germs from foul material get into the mouth if hands are not washed, causing stomach infections.

n.1: Standing near plant does not spread gastroenteritis.
n.2: Ill-fitting gloves are a nuisance but do not cause a stomach infection.
n.3: Looking at a joint cannot give you gastroenteritis.

9.q: Which is the best reason to treat any unidentified water in a trench as foul?
o: It saves the cost of testing the water before the job can continue
Assuming it is contaminated protects both the crew and the main
It gives the crew an excuse to finish the shift a little earlier
The water company always prefers extra paperwork to be completed
9.w: Treating unknown water as contaminated is the safe approach that protects the workers and the main.

n.0: Saving on testing is not the reason to assume the worst.
n.2: Finishing early is not a valid safety reason.
n.3: Paperwork preference has nothing to do with the real hazard.

9.q: If a water company finds coliforms in the supply, the appropriate response is to:
o: Ignore it, since coliforms are always harmless
Simply raise the temperature of the water
Investigate and act to protect consumers from contamination
Add extra minerals to improve the flavour
9.w: Finding coliforms should trigger investigation and protective action.

n.0: Coliforms are a warning and should not be ignored.
n.1: Raising temperature is not the correct response.
n.3: Adding minerals is not the correct response.

9.q: Why does a sudden drop in main pressure raise the contamination risk?
o: It can allow dirty water to be sucked back in
It makes the pipe walls become much thicker
It sterilises the whole inside of the main
It has no effect at all on contamination in practice
9.w: A pressure drop can cause backflow, sucking contaminated water into the main.

n.1: Pressure does not change wall thickness.
n.2: Low pressure does not sterilise anything.
n.3: Low pressure is a real backflow risk.

9.q: An operative caps a pipe end but the cap itself is caked in mud. The correct step is to:
o: Fit the muddy cap onto the end as it is as a rule
Skip the cap now that one has been found
Wipe the pipe end over with the muddy cap
Clean the cap before fitting it to the pipe
9.w: A cap must itself be clean, or it will contaminate the very end it is meant to protect.

n.0: A muddy cap carries contamination onto the pipe.
n.1: The end still needs a clean seal.
n.2: That spreads contamination onto the bore.

9.q: Which trench condition is acceptable for laying clean-water pipe?
o: A shallow layer of rainwater over the bed
A clean bed that has been de-watered
A trickle of foul water along the bottom
Soft mud with puddles between the stone
9.w: Pipe is only laid on a clean, de-watered bed so nothing contaminates the main.

n.0: Even a shallow layer of water is a contamination risk.
n.2: Any foul water in the trench is unacceptable.
n.3: Mud and puddles can contaminate the open pipe.

9.q: Which statement correctly links the offence and who can be charged?
o: Contaminating water can see an individual charged
Only the local councils can ever be charged
Contamination is never treated as a chargeable offence
Only the DWI itself can ever be charged
9.w: Contaminating drinking water is an offence for which an individual can be charged.

n.1: Councils are not the only ones; individuals can be charged.
n.2: It is a criminal offence and is chargeable.
n.3: The DWI is the regulator, not the offender.

9.q: PTFE tape used on drinking water threads should be:
o: a type approved for potable water use
wrapped around as many times as possible
any tape found loose in the tool bag
coloured to match the fitting nearby
9.w: Even PTFE tape must be an approved type suitable for drinking water.

n.1: The number of wraps does not make tape approved.
n.2: Random tape from the bag is not proof of approval.
n.3: Colour does not make tape approved for water.

10.q: When work stops for a break, open pipe ends should be:
o: left open so the pipe can dry inside
covered loosely with a handful of soil
capped or plugged to keep the inside clean
pointed downwards and simply left uncapped there
10.w: Capping or plugging every open end keeps dirt, water and vermin out while work is paused.

n.0: Leaving ends open lets contamination straight in.
n.1: Soil placed over the end is itself a contaminant.
n.3: Pointing down does not stop dirt or vermin entering.

10.q: Which of these best describes a Restricted Operation?
o: any task carried out near a water company site
any task that uses water company owned tools
any task that could contaminate the public supply
any task done during normal daytime working hours
10.w: A Restricted Operation is any task that could contaminate the supply.

n.0: Being near a site does not by itself make work restricted.
n.1: Using company tools does not define a restricted operation.
n.3: The time of day does not define a restricted operation.

10.q: Which of these best shows good awareness of contamination risk on site?
o: Opening up the main first and then looking around later
Ignoring any bad smells in order to keep to schedule on this job
Assuming the ground on every site is always kept clean
Checking the trench for foul water before opening the main
10.w: Checking the trench for foul water before opening the main shows proper risk awareness.

n.0: Checks come before opening.
n.1: Smells are warnings not to ignore.
n.2: Ground must be assessed, not assumed.

10.q: Capping open ends when work stops is important because the pipe is:
o: easier to store when the ends are shut
less likely to be stolen when capped
part of a supply people will drink from
protected from sunlight fading its colour
10.w: The main carries drinking water, so keeping its inside clean protects public health.

n.0: Storage is not the reason for capping on a live job.
n.1: Security is separate from the hygiene purpose.
n.3: Sun fading is not a drinking-water hygiene issue.

10.q: An operative is unsure whether a repaired section needs a sample before return. The best action is to:
o: Assume no sample is needed and return it to supply
Take no sample but keep an eye on customer complaints
Check the procedure and follow the sampling requirement
Return the main and arrange a sample only if problems arise
10.w: When unsure, the operative checks the procedure for that job and follows its sampling requirement before returning to supply.

n.0: Assuming no sample is needed risks returning unsafe water.
n.1: Waiting for complaints exposes the public first.
n.3: Sampling after problems arise is too late to protect consumers.

10.q: A key message of the National Water Hygiene scheme is that the law makes water protection:
o: A duty only for the largest of firms
A duty only during formal inspections
A personal duty for every operative
A duty that nobody can enforce
10.w: The scheme stresses that protecting water is a personal duty for every operative.

n.0: It applies to all who work on the network, not just large firms.
n.1: The duty applies all the time, not only at inspections.
n.3: The duty is enforceable, including by prosecution.

10.q: An operative must never fit an unapproved material even for a quick repair because it can:
o: contaminate the drinking water supply
void the manufacturer's tool warranty
make the repair take a little longer
use up more of the approved stock
10.w: Even a temporary unapproved fitting can contaminate the supply and is not allowed.

n.1: A tool warranty is not the safety reason it is banned.
n.2: Taking longer is not the safety reason it is banned.
n.3: Using stock is not the safety reason it is banned.

10.q: A workmate is about to eat a sandwich straight after clearing foul debris. You should:
o: Say nothing at all as it is entirely their own personal choice
Remind them just to wipe their hands on their overalls first
Tell them to wash their hands thoroughly before they eat
Suggest they eat quickly before the foul smell gets any worse
10.w: You tell them to wash their hands thoroughly first, so they do not swallow germs.

n.0: Staying silent leaves them at real risk of illness.
n.1: Wiping on overalls does not remove the germs.
n.3: Eating quickly does nothing to remove contamination.

10.q: Which action best protects water quality and meets the law at the same time?
o: Using approved fittings and reporting concerns
Using any handy spare part that will fit
Keeping quiet about a spillage that occurs
Reusing a tool that was dropped and dirtied
10.w: Using approved fittings and reporting concerns meets both hygiene and legal duties.

n.1: Unapproved parts can breach the fittings regulations.
n.2: Not reporting a spillage breaches personal responsibility.
n.3: A contaminated tool risks the water supply.

10.q: The Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 places general duties on:
o: Both employers and their employees
Only on employers, never on workers
Only on the members of the public
Only on the water quality regulator
10.w: The Act sets duties for employers and also requires employees to act safely.

n.1: Employees also carry duties under the Act, not employers alone.
n.2: The Act's duties fall mainly on those at work, not just the public.
n.3: The regulator does not carry the Act's workplace duties in place of employers.

10.q: A gang has no clean hand-washing facilities on site. What is the correct response?
o: Simply make use of the trench water to rinse your hands
Skip washing entirely until you eventually get home at night
Report it, as proper welfare facilities must be provided
Wipe your hands on your overalls and carry on eating anyway
10.w: Missing hand-washing facilities must be reported, as welfare must be provided.

n.0: Trench water may be contaminated and must never be used to wash.
n.1: Going all day without washing is unsafe; welfare must be provided.
n.3: Wiping on overalls does not clean hands; the issue must be reported.

10.q: Swabbing is carried out on a new main so that the later disinfection:
o: Acts on a clean pipe wall rather than being wasted on loose dirt and debris
Can be skipped entirely because the pipe is already known to be clean
Will set the joints hard so the main can be pressurised straight away
Produces a bright colour change that proves the water is now safe once the pipe has been rejoined
10.w: Clean pipework lets the chlorine reach the surfaces that matter instead of being used up by debris.

n.1: Swabbing supports disinfection; it does not remove the need to chlorinate.
n.2: Swabbing does not cure joints; that is unrelated to disinfection.
n.3: Swabbing removes solids; it does not produce a safety colour indicator.

10.q: The safest way to avoid material contamination on a new connection is to:
o: fit only approved materials throughout
fit the largest pipe that will fit
fit materials that match in colour
fit whatever type the customer happens to prefer
10.w: Fitting only approved materials throughout avoids contaminating the connection.

n.1: The largest pipe is not what avoids contamination.
n.2: Matching colour is not what avoids contamination.
n.3: Customer preference is not what avoids contamination.

10.q: A new potable main crosses close to an old sewer of unknown condition. The safe assumption is:
o: The sewer is fine because old sewers rarely give any real trouble
The two can safely share support as they are at a similar depth
No special precautions are needed as the main will be pressurised
The sewer may leak, so the water main must be protected from it
10.w: You assume the old sewer may leak, so the water main is protected and kept separated from it.

n.0: Assuming an old sewer is sound is not a safe assumption.
n.1: Sharing support removes the separation that is needed.
n.2: Pressure does not make it safe to skip precautions.

10.q: Scenario: a burst main has been repaired with a new section of pipe. Before it goes back into supply it should be:
o: Put back into supply at once because only a short section was replaced
Left to stand empty for a week so any germs die off by themselves
Disinfected, flushed and sampled because it was opened and could have been contaminated
Charged with extra pressure to force out any germs that got in as the work is being signed off
10.w: Opening the main for the repair means it must be disinfected and confirmed clean before use.

n.0: Even a short repair means the main was opened and must be disinfected.
n.1: Leaving it empty does not disinfect it; the proper procedure is required.
n.3: Pressure does not disinfect; chlorination and sampling are required.

10.q: A puddle has formed around the open end of a hose lying on the ground. Why is this a cross-connection concern?
o: The puddle keeps the hose end cool and prevents any risk
The puddle proves the main is already losing its pressure each time
The puddle water is filtered clean as it enters the hose
Dirty puddle water could be siphoned into the hose and the main
10.w: If the hose end sits in the puddle, a pressure drop could draw that contaminated water back into the supply.

n.0: Keeping the hose 'cool' is irrelevant; the risk is contamination.
n.1: A puddle is not evidence of mains pressure loss.
n.2: Puddle water is not filtered; entering the hose would pollute the supply.

10.q: If the trench keeps filling with water faster than you can bail, you should:
o: lay the pipe between the rising floods
set up pumping to keep the bed clear
give up de-watering and lay it wet
wait for the water to soak away on its own
10.w: Continuous inflow calls for proper pumping so the bed stays clear enough to lay clean pipe.

n.0: Laying between floods still puts pipe near foul water.
n.2: Laying it wet risks contaminating the main.
n.3: Waiting is not reliable when water keeps flowing in.

10.q: The golden rule for hoses on the potable supply is best stated as which?
o: Always leave the hose end resting in the water you are filling
Never let the hose end sit in the water you are filling
Only submerge the hose end when the pressure is high
Submerge the hose end but keep the tap almost closed
10.w: The rule is simple: keep the hose end out of the water, so it can never siphon back.

n.0: Leaving it in the water is exactly what causes the risk.
n.2: High pressure does not make submersion safe.
n.3: A nearly closed tap does not remove the submersion hazard.

10.q: Which of these would let leptospira enter the body most easily?
o: A clean and completely unbroken area of skin
A dry, dust-free and well-swept work surface
An uncovered cut or graze on the hand
A properly fitted and undamaged safety hard hat
10.w: An open cut or graze is a direct entry point for the organism.

n.0: Intact skin is a barrier; the organism enters through breaks in the skin.
n.1: A dry clean surface is not a route of entry into the body.
n.3: A hard hat protects the head and is not an entry point.

10.q: Which of these best protects both the worker and the water supply during breaks?
o: Washing hands before every break and after using the toilet
Keeping the work gloves on while eating your lunch
Giving the hands only a brief rinse under cold water
Using hand gel just the once at the end of the day
10.w: Washing before every break and after the toilet protects worker and supply alike.

n.1: Dirty gloves at lunch can still transfer organisms to food.
n.2: A brief cold rinse is not thorough hand washing.
n.3: One squirt of gel at day's end is not adequate hand hygiene.

10.q: Why is contamination of the public drinking water supply treated as a public-health emergency?
o: Because it always makes the water turn a bright colour
Because it can quickly make very large numbers of people ill
Because it slightly increases the cost shown on the water bill each year
Because it makes the pipes a little noisier than usual
10.w: Contaminated mains water can rapidly cause illness in many people.

n.0: Contamination is often invisible, not brightly coloured.
n.2: Cost is not why contamination is an emergency.
n.3: Noisy pipes are unrelated to a public-health emergency.

10.q: Which of these describes contamination entering a main by backflow?
o: Clean, treated water pushed out to a customer's tap
Water flowing normally down along the pipe
Trapped air venting from a high point valve
Non-potable water siphoned back into the main
10.w: Backflow is non-potable water being drawn back into the main against the normal flow.

n.0: That is normal forward supply.
n.1: Normal flow is not backflow.
n.2: Venting air is not backflow of dirty water.

10.q: Why is it fair to say the consequences of backflow fall on the whole community, not just one site?
o: The contaminated water can be delivered to every connected property
Only the operative who caused it ever drinks the bad water
The water company keeps the incident secret from all customers each time
The pollution is billed evenly across the district accounts
10.w: Because the network is shared, the results of a backflow event can reach all the properties fed by that main.

n.1: The person at fault is not the only one exposed to the risk.
n.2: Companies must warn affected customers, not hide the incident.
n.3: Consequences are about health, not how costs are billed.

10.q: An operative is called away mid-job with a pipe end open. They should first:
o: Leave it and just deal with it later in most cases
Lay the open end down in trench water
Cap or plug the open end before leaving
Throw a rag loosely over the open end
10.w: Before leaving, the open end must be properly capped or plugged.

n.0: Leaving it open invites contamination.
n.1: That directly contaminates the pipe.
n.3: A loose rag is not a proper seal.

10.q: How is a new or repaired main normally disinfected before it goes into supply?
o: By heating the pipe until any organisms inside are killed by the temperature
By leaving the empty pipe open to fresh air for several dry days
By coating the inside of the pipe with a thick layer of grease while the job is being carried out
By dosing the water with chlorine to a set concentration and holding it for a contact time
10.w: Chlorination to a specified strength, held for the required time, is the standard disinfection method.

n.0: Mains are disinfected chemically by chlorination, not by heating the pipe.
n.1: Air-drying does not disinfect a main; chlorinated water is used.
n.2: Grease does not disinfect; chlorination of the water is the method.
